cases.promptMarkdown:
Review this copy. The device is a Class IIa continuous ECG patch. Intended
purpose as assessed: "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the
supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac
arrhythmias."

Copy: "The X100 patch records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight. New parents love
it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight, just peel, stick, and sleep."

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
The device's assessed intended purpose is continuous single-lead ECG recording **in
adults**, **under healthcare-professional supervision**, for **detecting cardiac
arrhythmias**. The copy sells overnight breathing monitoring of a **newborn** by a
**parent**.

PASS requires:
(1) The newborn breathing-monitoring use is flagged as a breach of **MDR Art. 7(d)**,
    suggesting a use outside the assessed intended purpose. Art. 7(d) must be named.
(2) It is NOT treated as a truthfulness problem, and NOT said to be curable by evidence
    or substantiation. The cure is narrowing the claim or extending the conformity
    assessment.
(3) At least one of the three drifts is named explicitly: newborn vs "in adults";
    breathing vs cardiac-arrhythmia ECG; unsupervised parental use vs HCP supervision.

Also flagging Art. 7(a) or 7(b) alongside (d) is correct and does not cost the pass
respiration monitoring is not in the assessed purpose, and positioning the patch as an
infant breathing monitor creates a false impression regarding diagnosis.

Note for the judge: the reference file's own limb (d) example uses a different scenario.
Do not look for that wording; judge whether the reasoning is applied to THIS copy.

Additionally, no market is stated in this prompt. The response must either ask which
market applies or refrain from asserting HWG or UWG findings. Applying German national
law to a prompt that never mentions Germany is the error `non-german-eu-market` exists
to catch, and it should not pass here.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — consumer copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch, Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** **Publikum.** "your heart rhythm", "New parents" — consumer-directed, no gating implied. HWG § 11 applies (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only) *if* the German market is in scope.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **German market not stated** — MDR Art. 7 findings below stand regardless; HWG/UWG items are recorded as `Also engaged` conditional on DE targeting. Tell me if DE is in scope and I'll promote them.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. **2 cut, 2 reword, 0 substantiate, 0 OK.** 1 item to verify.

**Ready to publish: No, rewrite needed.**

The newborn-breathing sentence is the serious one: it breaches MDR Art. 7(a), (b) and (d) simultaneously, and **limb (d) cannot be cured by evidence** — no study makes neonatal respiration monitoring part of an intended purpose assessed for adult ECG arrhythmia detection. It has to be cut or the conformity assessment extended. The consumer/self-use framing across the rest of the copy is a second, independent (d) problem: the assessed purpose has healthcare-professional supervision built into it, and this copy removes it.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)**, **7(a)**, **7(b)** [verified]
**Why:**
- **(d)** "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out" — three separate drifts in one clause: population (newborn vs. **adults**), indication (breathing vs. **ECG / cardiac arrhythmias**), and setting (parental overnight monitoring at home vs. **under the supervision of a healthcare professional**).
- **(a)** "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have" — respiration monitoring is not a function within the assessed purpose, which covers single-lead ECG recording.
- **(b)** "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis" — a parent reads this as the device watching for a newborn's breathing stopping. That is a safety-critical monitoring impression an adult arrhythmia recorder does not deliver.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Curable only by cutting the claim or extending the conformity assessment to a neonatal respiration indication (different population, different indication; a new assessment, not a data annex).
**Also engaged:** if DE market — **HWG § 3 no. 1** (Wirkungen beigelegt, die sie nicht haben) [verified]; **HWG § 11(1) no. 7**, health "durch die Verwendung verbessert"/impaired by non-use — protecting a sleeping newborn is that framing at its strongest [verified]; **HWG § 11(1) no. 11** *if* "new parents love it" is rendered as actual customer statements, since the use they endorse is irreführend [verified]; **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** Zwecktauglichkeit / Verwendungsmöglichkeit [verified].
**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** Delete entirely. If you need a reassurance beat for the consumer audience, it has to sit inside the assessed purpose — see the rewritten copy below.

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)** [verified]
**Why:** Same limb (d) operative words. The assessed intended purpose is qualified by "under the supervision of a healthcare professional". A three-step self-application instruction with no clinical actor in it suggests unsupervised consumer self-use — a setting outside what was assessed. Read together with the preceding sentence it also carries the (b) reassurance ("sleep" = sleep safely).
**Evidence needed:** n/a — intended-purpose scope, not a substantiation question.
**Also engaged:** if DE market — **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** (Verwendungsmöglichkeit).
**Call:** **Reword** — keep the ease-of-use benefit, restore the supervision condition.
**Suggested fix:** "Simple to apply, and set up with your healthcare professional."

---

**Claim:** "The X100 patch records **your** heart rhythm"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)** [verified]
**Why:** Second-person consumer address with no prescriber or professional in the frame suggests a direct-to-consumer self-monitoring use. The supervision condition is part of the intended purpose as assessed, not an optional add-on, so dropping it suggests a use beyond that purpose. This is a lighter version of the same defect as the claim above, and it is fixed by wording rather than by cutting.
**Evidence needed:** n/a.
**Call:** **Reword.**
**Suggested fix:** "The X100 patch records a continuous single-lead ECG, prescribed and reviewed by your healthcare professional."

---

**Claim:** "for 14 days straight"
**Breach:** **none** on the material supplied.
**Why:** A duration claim consistent with a continuous-recording device. Nothing in the intended purpose contradicts it.
**Evidence needed:** maximum validated wear time from the technical documentation / IFU. If the validated figure is "up to 14 days" or shorter under some skin or adhesive conditions, "14 days straight" overstates it and becomes **Art. 7(a)** (and **UWG § 5(2) no. 1**, von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse).
**Also engaged:** **MDR Art. 7(a)**, if validated wear time is below 14 days or is conditional.
**Call:** **Verify.**
**Suggested fix (safe form pending the file):** "records for up to 14 days".

---

## Open question on limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation at all — no mention that ECG recordings require clinical interpretation, and no contraindication or age restriction. I am **not** raising an Art. 7(c) finding, for two reasons: (c) is limited by its own words to "a likely risk associated with the use of the device **in line with its intended purpose**", and I have not seen the IFU, so I cannot name the risk from supplied material. Worth checking the IFU for a paediatric exclusion and any skin/adhesive or arrhythmia-detection limitation, and whether one of them belongs in consumer-facing copy of this length.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated maximum continuous wear time, and any conditions on it | Regulatory / technical file owner |
| (limb (c) question) | IFU contraindications — paediatric/neonatal exclusion, interpretation requirement | Regulatory / IFU author |
| Market scope | Is DE targeted? Determines whether the HWG and UWG items above are live | Marketing |

## Paste-ready rewrite

> The X100 patch records a continuous single-lead ECG for up to 14 days. Prescribed and set up with your healthcare professional, it gives them the recording they need to detect cardiac arrhythmias. Simple to apply, and comfortable to sleep in. For adults only — the X100 is not a breathing or apnoea monitor and is not for use on children or infants.

Two notes on that draft. "up to 14 days" is placeholder until the wear-time figure is confirmed. The explicit "not a breathing or apnoea monitor" line is there because once the newborn framing has been used in market, an express exclusion is the cheapest way to unwind the impression — drop it if this copy never ran.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 1 — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11 — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — short-form marketing copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch, Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Publikum. "your heart rhythm", "new parents", "peel, stick, and sleep" is consumer-facing on its face; no Fachkreise reading is available.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **Germany not confirmed** — HWG/UWG findings below are conditional and marked as such.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.**

The newborn sentence is the whole review. It breaches three of the four Art. 7 limbs at once, and it is the kind of breach evidence cannot cure: the intended purpose says **adults**, and it says **ECG for arrhythmia detection**, not respiration. A clinical study showing the patch happens to pick up respiratory signal in infants would not fix this claim — only narrowing the copy, or extending the conformity assessment to a new population and a new indication, would.

The secondary problem runs through the rest of the copy: "peel, stick, and sleep" drops the healthcare-professional supervision that is written into the assessed intended purpose, repositioning a supervised clinical device as a consumer self-care product.

**Ready to publish:** No, rewrite needed.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d), Art. 7(a), Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". Two independent departures in one clause: a **population** the assessment does not cover (newborns; intended purpose reads "in adults") and an **indication** it does not cover (breathing monitoring; intended purpose reads ECG recording for detection of cardiac arrhythmias). Either alone breaches (d).
- **(a)** — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". Respiration monitoring is presented as a function of the patch. A single-lead ECG recorder assessed for arrhythmia detection has no assessed respiratory-monitoring function.
- **(b)** — "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis". "Keeping an eye on... overnight" invites parents to rely on the patch as unattended infant breathing surveillance while they sleep. That is a false impression of a monitoring capability, and it attaches to the highest-consequence possible reader.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Limb (d) is not a truthfulness test; the anchor is the assessed intended purpose, not what the device can factually do. Cure is to delete the claim, or to extend the conformity assessment to the paediatric population and a respiratory indication.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — third-party statements ("New parents love it") where made "in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder **irreführender** Weise". Testimonials are not banned for devices; this one is misleading because what the third parties are said to endorse is an unassessed use. Conditional on the German market.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse". Conditional on the German market. This is the route by which the above arrives as an **Abmahnung** with costs rather than a regulator's letter.

**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** Delete the sentence entirely. There is no narrowed version that keeps the intent — the intent *is* the off-purpose use.

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** The assessed intended purpose is qualified: "**under the supervision of a healthcare professional**". Copy that frames the whole interaction as self-applied and self-managed suggests a use — unsupervised consumer self-monitoring — outside the assessed purpose. The qualifying condition is part of the intended purpose, not packaging around it.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by restoring the condition, not by data.
**Call:** **Reword.**
**Suggested fix:** "Simple to apply, and comfortable to wear overnight — fitted and reviewed as part of your clinician's monitoring plan."

---

**Claim:** "The X100 patch records your heart rhythm" (second-person, direct-to-consumer framing)
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`, on the framing rather than the fact
**Why:** The recording function itself is accurate and within the intended purpose. The breach risk is the second-person consumer address with no mention that the recording exists to be **interpreted by a clinician** for arrhythmia detection. Standing alone it reads as a self-service heart check — a false impression regarding diagnosis. Note this finding is largely absorbed if the fix to "peel, stick, and sleep" is adopted, since that restores the supervision context.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — resolved by context, not data.
**Call:** **Reword** (together with the line above).
**Suggested fix:** Handled in the consolidated rewrite below.

---

**Claim:** "records your heart rhythm for **14 days straight**"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Continuous recording is squarely within the assessed intended purpose. The figure "14 days" is a specific performance claim that I have not seen substantiated — but an unsubstantiated-on-the-material-supplied figure is an open question for the technical file, not a breach of the operative words of any provision in front of me.
**Evidence needed:** Maximum validated wear duration from the IFU and the wear-time / adhesion / signal-quality data in the technical documentation. Confirm 14 days is the **validated continuous** figure, not a best case or a battery-life figure.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`, **if** the validated continuous wear time is shorter than 14 days or is conditional (e.g. skin type, adhesive replacement).
**Call:** **Verify.**
**Suggested fix:** None needed if the figure holds. If it is conditional, state the condition: "up to 14 days of continuous recording".

---

### Open question I am not raising as a finding

**Limb (c) — failing to inform of a likely risk.** The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I am **not** recording this as a breach, for a specific reason: limb (c) covers risks "associated with the use of the device **in line with its intended purpose**", and the newborn use is by definition not in line with it — so the infant-reliance hazard is caught by (a), (b) and (d), not by (c). Whether there is a likely in-purpose risk that belongs in this copy (skin irritation from 14-day adhesive wear, contraindications, the fact that recordings require clinical interpretation) I cannot tell from what I have. **Worth checking against the IFU.** For a 35-word asset an IFU pointer is usually the proportionate fix if one bites.

## Paste-ready rewrite

> The X100 patch records your heart rhythm continuously for up to 14 days, so your clinician can review it for signs of arrhythmia. Simple to apply and comfortable to wear overnight. For use in adults, as part of a monitoring plan supervised by a healthcare professional.

What this keeps: the 14 days, the ease-of-use benefit, the overnight-wear benefit, the consumer-readable tone. What it drops: the newborn use, and the implication that the patch is something you interpret yourself. If the IFU records a likely risk, append a "See the instructions for use" pointer.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated maximum **continuous** wear duration; whether conditional | Regulatory / technical documentation owner |
| Whole asset | Whether the IFU records a likely risk (adhesive/skin, contraindications, need for clinical interpretation) that belongs in patient-facing copy | Regulatory / IFU owner |
| Whole asset | Confirm target market — Germany yes/no. Two conditional findings turn on this | Marketing |
| "New parents love it" | n/a — the claim is cut, not substantiated | — |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d)** `[verified]` — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md`
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11** `[verified]` — `references/hwg.md` (devices: only nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 apply; Publikum only)
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** `[verified]` — `references/uwg.md`

Not engaged, for the record: **UWG § 6** (no comparison in the copy); **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** (no certification, class or notified-body claim made); **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)/(b)** (no guarantee of success, no no-side-effects claim); **HWG § 3a** (Arzneimittel only, never applies to devices).

I considered **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** (health impaired by non-use / improved by use) for the newborn sentence and am not recording it. The copy implies reassurance from use, but it does not assert that health is impaired by not using the patch, and no. 7's operative words need that framing. The sentence is cut on Art. 7 grounds regardless.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — short-form marketing copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch, Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias"
**Audience:** Publikum. "your heart rhythm" and "new parents" address consumers directly, so HWG § 11 (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only) would apply on the German market.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **DE not confirmed** — the HWG/UWG findings below are recorded as `Also engaged` and become live breaches if this runs in Germany. Tell me and I will promote them.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 2 cut, 1 reword/substantiate, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No, rewrite needed.**

The second sentence is the serious one. It moves the device to a population the conformity assessment did not cover (newborns, not adults), to a physiological parameter the device does not measure (respiration, not cardiac rhythm), and to an unsupervised home-safety-monitoring use. None of that is fixable with data.

---

## Findings

### 1. Newborn breathing monitoring — **Cut**

**Claim:** "New parents love it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". The assessed purpose is **adults**. Newborns are a different population, and infant use is a different risk profile entirely.
- **(a)** — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". A single-lead ECG recorder indicated for arrhythmia detection is not a respiration monitor. Breathing is not in the assessed purpose.
- **(b)** — "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis". "Keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" reads as overnight infant safety surveillance. That is a clinical impression the device does not support, and it is the kind of impression a parent acts on by not checking.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. (d) is cured only by deleting the use or extending the conformity assessment; new respiration data would not cure (a) either, since adding respiration would itself be an intended-purpose extension.
**Also engaged (DE market only):** HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]` — "Wirkungen beigelegt werden, die sie nicht haben". HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — "Äußerungen Dritter … wenn diese in … irreführender Weise erfolgen"; "new parents love it" is a third-party endorsement carrying precisely the misleading use. HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` if the infant-safety framing is read as suggesting health is safeguarded by use. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit".
**Call:** Cut.
**Suggested fix:** Delete the sentence. There is no narrowed version of it, the population and the parameter are both outside scope.

### 2. "just peel, stick, and sleep" — **Cut or reword**

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — the assessed purpose is qualified "under the supervision of a healthcare professional". Self-application-and-forget framing suggests unsupervised consumer use, which drops a condition the conformity assessment was carried out against.
- **(c)** — "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose". The supervision requirement is in the assessed intended purpose you supplied; copy that presents the device as a standalone consumer product omits that the recording exists to be clinically interpreted. I am anchoring (c) on that supplied condition only, not on an inferred device-category risk.

**Evidence needed:** n/a for (d). For (c), an IFU pointer plus the supervision context is the proportionate fix at this length.
**Also engaged (DE market only):** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "Verwendungsmöglichkeit".
**Call:** Needs rewording.
**Suggested fix:** Keep the ease-of-wear point, restore the supervision frame: "Applied once and worn continuously — your clinician reviews the recording."

### 3. 14-day recording — **Verify**

**Claim:** "The X100 patch records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied. "Heart rhythm" is acceptable lay phrasing for single-lead ECG, and continuous recording is the assessed purpose.
**Evidence needed:** the validated maximum wear time and continuous-recording duration from the technical documentation. If the assessed wear time is shorter, or 14 days depends on conditions (skin prep, replacement adhesive, battery), the unqualified figure becomes MDR Art. 7(a) and, on the German market, UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]`, if 14 days is not the assessed figure and the market is DE.
**Call:** Verify.
**Suggested fix:** As written, subject to the technical file confirming 14 days unqualified. Otherwise: "records continuously for up to 14 days".

**Drafting note (not a finding):** sentence 1 addresses the reader as the wearer ("your heart rhythm"), sentence 2 puts it on a newborn. Even setting the regulatory problem aside, the asset does not identify a consistent user.

---

## Paste-ready rewrite

> The X100 patch records a continuous single-lead ECG for up to 14 days. Prescribed and reviewed by your healthcare professional to help detect cardiac arrhythmias in adults. Applied once, worn day and night. Read the instructions for use.

40 words in, 38 out. It keeps the duration, the ease-of-wear point, and the consumer register, and it drops the two uses the conformity assessment does not cover.

---

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated continuous wear/recording duration; any conditions attached | Regulatory / technical documentation owner |
| Whole asset | Does the IFU record a likely risk (skin reaction, data gaps, need for clinical interpretation) that belongs in patient-facing copy at this length? I cannot tell from what I have. | Regulatory affairs |
| Market | Is this running in Germany? Determines whether the HWG/UWG items above are live | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

No comparison in the copy, so UWG § 6 is not engaged. No certification, class or notified-body claim, so UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 are not engaged.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

## Verdict: do not publish

Two of the three sentences make claims outside the assessed intended purpose. This is not a wording problem you can soften — the newborn-breathing claim has to come out entirely.

## Findings

**1. Newborn respiration monitoring — critical (remove, do not reword)**

"keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" breaks the intended purpose on three axes at once:

- **Function:** the device records single-lead ECG. It does not monitor respiration. Promoting a function the device does not have breaches MDR Art. 7(1)(a) and (b).
- **Population:** assessed for adults. No paediatric/neonatal clinical evaluation, and neonatal HR (~120–160 bpm) sits outside the range adult arrhythmia algorithms are typically validated for. Electrode spacing, patch size and adhesive are also unvalidated on neonatal skin.
- **Classification:** respiration monitoring in a neonate is monitoring of a vital parameter where variation means immediate danger — Annex VIII Rule 10 puts that in **Class IIb**, not IIa. The claim describes a device your certificate does not cover.

The foreseeable harm is the real problem: a parent who reads this may substitute the patch for apnoea surveillance. That is a failure-to-rescue scenario, and the copy would be Exhibit A in the resulting claim. It also creates a foreseeable misuse you'd then owe a risk-management and PMS response to.

**2. "just peel, stick, and sleep" — must change**

The assessed purpose requires use *under the supervision of a healthcare professional*. This phrasing positions the device as lay-use consumer wellness tech and drops the supervision condition. Omitting a condition of the intended purpose is itself misleading under Annex I Ch. III §23.1.

**3. "New parents love it" — unsubstantiated**

A popularity/testimonial claim with no evidence behind it, attached to a population the device isn't indicated for. Remove. If you want social proof, it has to be substantiated and tied to the indicated population (adults, HCP-supervised).

**4. "14 days straight" — substantiate or qualify**

Defensible only if verification data supports 14 days of *uninterrupted* recording in the worst case: battery life, memory, and validated adhesive wear time, including any planned patch change. If wear time is "up to 14 days" or requires a mid-wear replacement, say so. Check this against the technical documentation before release.

**5. Omissions**

No mention that it's single-lead, that it's a recorder reviewed by a clinician rather than a real-time alarm, or that it does not detect all arrhythmias. Silence on the real-time point is what lets readers assume live monitoring.

## Suggested rewrite

> The X100 is a single-lead ECG patch prescribed by your healthcare professional to record your heart rhythm for up to 14 days. It is worn on the chest and records continuously, day and night, so your clinician can review the recording for signs of cardiac arrhythmia.
>
> For use in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional. The X100 records your ECG for later clinical review — it is not a real-time monitor and does not raise alarms. It does not monitor breathing and is not intended for use in infants or children.

Swap "up to 14 days" for "14 days" only if verification data supports the worst case unqualified.

## Before release

- Confirm the 14-day wear-time claim against verification/validation data, and log the claim-to-evidence link in your claims substantiation matrix.
- Add "use as an infant breathing/apnoea monitor" to the risk file as foreseeable misuse, if it isn't there — the fact that marketing reached for it is evidence the misuse is foreseeable.
- If neonatal or respiration use is genuinely a commercial target, that is a new intended purpose: notified body review, paediatric clinical evaluation, and re-classification to IIb. Not a copy edit.
- Check national advertising rules in your target member states; several restrict promotion of prescription/HCP-supervised devices to the general public, which this copy is squarely aimed at.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish. Two claims fall outside the assessed intended purpose, and one of them implies a different (higher-risk) device.

### Findings, by severity

**1. Neonatal use — off-label population (critical)**
"keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing" promotes use in a population the intended purpose explicitly excludes ("in adults"). Nothing in your technical documentation, clinical evaluation, or usability work covers neonates — different skin, different adhesive tolerance, different arrhythmia profile, different electrode geometry. Under MDR Article 7 this is a misleading claim; more seriously, promoting a device for a purpose outside its stated intended purpose can be read as placing a *different* device on the market, with all the conformity-assessment consequences that implies.

**2. Respiration monitoring — function the device does not have (critical)**
The device records single-lead ECG. It does not measure respiration. Even if you derive an ECG-derived respiration signal, that is not in the assessed intended purpose and cannot be claimed. Worse, "keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" reads unmistakably as an infant apnea/SIDS monitor. That function is monitoring a vital physiological process where variation could cause immediate danger — Class IIb territory under MDR Rule 10, not IIa — and a parent could reasonably delay seeking help because they believe the patch is watching. This is the exact harm MDR Article 7(b) and (d) target.

**3. "just peel, stick, and sleep" — drops the HCP supervision condition (major)**
The intended purpose is conditioned on "under the supervision of a healthcare professional." The copy positions the device as a standalone consumer product with no clinician in the loop, and implies the output requires no interpretation. The supervision condition has to survive into the marketing, not just sit in the IFU.

**4. "New parents love it" — unsubstantiated testimonial (major)**
Beyond reinforcing the off-label population, generalised testimonial claims need substantiation, and testimonials in medical device advertising are restricted or prohibited in several Member States. Drop it.

**5. "14 days straight" — verify, don't assume (minor, evidence-dependent)**
Defensible only if 14 days continuous wear is the validated wear time in your technical documentation and IFU, including adhesive and skin-irritation testing at that duration. If the IFU says "up to 14 days" or requires a patch change, "14 days straight" overstates it. Also note there is no arrhythmia-detection claim anywhere in the copy — the actual approved purpose is missing while two unapproved ones are present.

### Suggested rewrite

> The X100 is a wearable patch that continuously records your single-lead ECG for up to 14 days, helping your doctor detect cardiac arrhythmias. Prescribed and monitored by a healthcare professional, it's applied once and worn discreetly, day and night.
>
> For use in adults only. The X100 records ECG for review by a healthcare professional; it does not measure breathing and does not provide diagnoses or alerts. Not for use in children or infants.

Adjust the trailing disclaimer to your usual format, and add the CE mark, manufacturer, and "read the instructions for use" per your labelling SOP and the channel's requirements.

### Before sign-off, confirm

- Validated continuous wear duration in the IFU matches whatever number you publish.
- No respiration or apnea functionality is claimed anywhere else in the campaign (web, packaging, app store listing, sales decks) — if this copy reached a writer, the framing may be elsewhere too.
- Whether the "newborn breathing" angle originated as a product-roadmap ambition. If someone intends to pursue it, that is a new intended purpose, a likely Class IIb classification, and fresh clinical evidence — worth raising with regulatory affairs now rather than after a launch.

One thing I couldn't check: point 5 depends on your actual IFU wear-time wording and adhesive test data. If you paste the relevant IFU section I'll confirm whether "up to 14 days" is the right phrasing.

## Verdict: Do not publish. Two claims are off-label; one is a safety hazard.

**Findings, worst first**

1. **"keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" — off-label on two axes at once, and unsafe.**
   - *Population:* intended purpose is **adults**. Neonates are excluded, and a single-lead adult patch has no validated performance in that population (electrode size/spacing, adhesive on neonatal skin, HR range).
   - *Function:* the device records **ECG for arrhythmia detection**. It does not measure respiration. Promoting it as a breathing monitor creates the impression of a function the device does not have — squarely MDR Art. 7(a)/(b).
   - *Harm pathway:* parents may rely on it as an apnoea/SIDS monitor and not seek care or use a validated monitor. This is the kind of claim that draws a competent-authority action, not just a warning letter, and it would likely be read as a significant change in intended purpose requiring new conformity assessment if you actually wanted to make it.

2. **"just peel, stick, and sleep" — contradicts the assessed intended purpose.** The device is certified for use *under the supervision of a healthcare professional*. Copy that frames it as a self-serve consumer product removes the HCP from the loop and misleads on conditions of use.

3. **"New parents love it" — unsubstantiated testimonial-style claim** for an unapproved use. Even if you fixed the indication, aggregate preference claims need evidence on file.

4. **"14 days straight" — substantiate or soften.** Only claim the wear duration validated in your technical documentation (adhesive, battery, signal quality to end of wear). If 14 days is the tested maximum rather than the typical, say "up to 14 days."

5. **Omission:** no statement of the actual purpose (arrhythmia detection) and no HCP/prescription framing. Art. 7 covers misleading by omission as well as by assertion.

**Compliant rewrite**

> The X100 patch continuously records a single-lead ECG for up to 14 days, giving your clinician the data they need to detect cardiac arrhythmias. Prescribed and reviewed by a healthcare professional. For use in adults. The X100 does not monitor breathing and is not intended for use in infants or children.

Notes on the rewrite: "up to 14 days" pending your wear-duration evidence; the final sentence is a deliberate contraindication statement — if the newborn angle has already been used in market, keep it, otherwise it can move to the IFU and off the ad.

**What I'd need to close this out:** the validated wear duration from the technical file, and confirmation of whether "supervision of a healthcare professional" in your assessed purpose means prescription-only in your target markets — that changes whether consumer-facing advertising is permissible at all for this device.

One scope note: this is an editorial/regulatory-risk review against the intended purpose you gave me. It isn't a sign-off from your PRRC or notified body, and final claim wording should go through them.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: gated procurement page, testimonial + install-base block

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Surgical navigation system, Class IIb (as stated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise. Credentialed login, hospital procurement and clinical engineering — both sit inside Fachkreise per `references/hwg.md` § Fachkreise vs. Publikum. **HWG § 11 does not apply.** § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (copy also claims AT and CH presence)

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 0 substantiate, 2 verify.

**No breach established on the material supplied.** Both rewords are presentation risk, not provisions the copy conflicts with as written. The substance of this review is four verification items and two scoping fixes.

**Ready to publish: With changes below.**

One false positive to head off first, because it is the likely reflex on this copy: a named professor at a university hospital endorsing a device is **not** a § 11(1) no. 2 problem. No. 2 (Empfehlung von Angehörigen der Heilberufe) does not apply to medical devices at all — `references/hwg.md` records that only nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 apply — and § 11 is switched off entirely here by the credentialed gate. Nor is the testimonial caught by no. 11, which bites only where a third-party statement is missbräuchlich, abstoßend or irreführend. Don't let anyone cut this on § 11 grounds.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A workflow-step reduction is a factual, checkable property, and nothing in the material supplied contradicts it. The risk is in the word **"every"**: a single clinician's experience at one site is quoted in wording that asserts an invariant property of the device. If the two steps come out for every user in every configuration, the claim is sound. If the reduction is specific to that site's prior workflow, anatomy mix, or configuration, the same sentence becomes a capability stated without its qualifying condition — the classic MDR Art. 7(a) shape `[verified]` — and an inaccurate statement about "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`.
**Evidence needed:** Whether the step reduction is inherent to the registration workflow or site-specific. From product management, against the workflow as documented.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a); UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if the reduction is site- or configuration-dependent rather than inherent.
**Call:** Needs rewording — scope the quote to its source so the claim does not depend on the answer.
**Suggested fix:** see block below.

---

**Claim:** "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Accurate on its face if the install base supports it. Two soft spots. "**Routine use**" excludes pilots, evaluations and loan units — if any of the DACH sites are in those categories, this is an overstated track record under HWG § 3 no. 3(b) ("Erfolge des Herstellers") `[verified]` and a misleading statement about wesentliche Merkmale under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`. "**Across the DACH region**" reads as all three countries — if it is Germany plus one Austrian site, the phrase overstates coverage on the same two provisions.
**Evidence needed:** Site list by country, with each site's status (routine clinical use vs. pilot/evaluation) and go-live date. From sales operations. Date-stamp the figure.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 (Zulassung of the goods) `[verified]` — if a reader of this page would take "in routine use across DACH" as an assertion that the device is lawfully marketable in all three countries and that is not the case for one of them. Switzerland is outside the EU, so the CE certificate does not by itself answer this; the Swiss requirements are outside what this skill verifies `[verify]` — confirm with regulatory affairs before the sentence goes out naming CH.
**Call:** Needs rewording — name the countries and the site count rather than a region label.
**Suggested fix:** see block below.

---

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Nothing misleading on the material supplied. But "Universitätsklinikum Süd" does not correspond to a German university hospital I can identify, which suggests it is either a placeholder in this draft or an anonymised site. An anonymised or invented institution presented as a named, real reference is zur Täuschung geeignet about a wesentliches Merkmal of the offer — UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — because the whole persuasive force of the line is that a procurement reader can place the institution.
**Evidence needed:** (1) Is the institution name real and is this the form it has approved? (2) Written consent from Prof. Ellwanger and the Klinikum for name, title, affiliation and the exact quote. (3) Any commercial relationship between Prof. Ellwanger and the manufacturer — consultancy, speaker fees, advisory board, equity, study funding.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(c) (false impression that the material is not for competitive purposes) and § 3 no. 3(b) (statements about persons working or having worked for the manufacturer) `[verified]` — both if a paid relationship exists and is not disclosed. On a gated page the promotional purpose is otherwise plain, so disclosure of the relationship is the fix, not removal of the quote.
**Call:** Verify — do not publish until the institution name and the consent are confirmed.

---

**Claim:** "since 2024"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A duration claim. Checkable, and correct or not on the facts.
**Evidence needed:** Date of first routine clinical installation, not first pilot or first shipment.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — if the 2024 anchor date is a pilot or a pre-CE evaluation rather than routine use.
**Call:** Verify.

---

## Open question I cannot close: limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation, and the specific thing it celebrates is **removing steps from registration** — the step in navigation where accuracy is established. That makes limb (c) worth a deliberate check rather than a shrug. But I will not raise it as a finding: I have not seen the IFU, and MDR Art. 7(c) requires a **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose `[verified]`. Inferring one from the device category would give you an unfalsifiable finding.

So, as an open question for regulatory affairs: **does the IFU record a registration-accuracy verification step, or a warning about relying on registration without verification?** If it does, this copy invites a reader to hear "two fewer steps" as "two fewer checks," and an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix. If it does not, there is nothing to add.

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

English, matching the draft. Bracketed values need filling from the verification items above.

> Prof. [full name], [department], [full institution name]: "In our workflow, two steps came out of every registration." — single-site user report; the number of steps depends on the local workflow and configuration.
>
> [Product] has been in routine clinical use at [N] hospitals in Germany, Austria and Switzerland since [month] 2024 (as of September 2026).

Add, **only if** the IFU records a verification step:

> Registration accuracy must be verified by the user in accordance with the instructions for use.

Add, **if** a commercial relationship exists:

> Prof. [name] is a paid [advisor/consultant] to [manufacturer].

Three notes on the fix. First, "two steps came out of every registration" keeps the clinician's meaning while the appositive makes the scope of the observation explicit, so the sentence no longer asserts an invariant. Second, naming the three countries and the site count replaces a region label that reads broader than most install bases actually are, and it is cheap to defend — a narrow verifiable number costs far less than a broad true one, which is the practical calculus behind an Abmahnung. Third, the date stamp matters: install-base claims go stale silently, and a stamped figure ages into "out of date" rather than into "misleading."

Whether German-language copy is required for this market is a labelling-language question outside the provisions this skill verifies `[verify]` — worth asking regulatory affairs, since the page is German-market and currently in English.

## If the gate ever comes off

The Fachkreise finding is doing real work here, and it is the first thing that breaks if this copy is reused. Un-gate the page, or lift these two sentences into a brochure, a trade-show panel, or anything a patient can reach, and HWG § 11(1) reopens: no. 11 on the testimonial (misleading only), no. 9 if the promotional purpose stops being obvious, no. 7 on any health-improvement framing `[verified]`. Flag the copy as Fachkreise-only in the asset register.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "two steps out of every registration" | Is the reduction inherent to the workflow or site-specific? | Product management |
| "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd" | Real institution name; written consent for name, title, quote | Marketing / the Klinikum |
| same | Disclosure of any commercial relationship | Legal / medical affairs |
| "in routine use" / "across the DACH region" | Site list by country with status (routine vs. pilot) | Sales operations |
| "since 2024" | Date of first routine clinical installation | Sales operations |
| DACH marketability | Confirmation the device is lawfully marketable in DE, AT and CH | Regulatory affairs |
| Limb (c) | Does the IFU record a registration-accuracy verification step? | Regulatory affairs |

## Not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

Two things I would look at specifically once I have it. A Class IIb navigation system's assessed intended purpose is usually confined to named anatomical regions and procedure types; "in routine use across the DACH region" says nothing about indication, so it is probably clean, but the surrounding page is where drift shows up. And Prof. Ellwanger's specialty, once the attribution is complete, will imply a procedure type to any procurement reader — if that procedure sits outside the assessed intended purpose, the testimonial suggests it, and a limb (d) breach of that kind is cured by narrowing the claim, not by evidence.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), 7(c) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(c), § 3 no. 3(b), § 11(1) nos. 2, 7, 9, 11 (scoping) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 5(2) no. 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- Swiss marketability requirements; German labelling-language requirements — `[verify]`, outside this skill's references

UWG § 6 is **not** engaged. "Two steps out of every registration" implies a baseline, but the baseline is that site's own prior workflow, and no competitor is erkennbar within § 6(1) `[verified]`. That changes if the prior system at the reference site is named anywhere on the page, or if the DACH navigation market can tell who is meant — at that point the undefined comparator would breach § 6(2) no. 2 on the face of the copy, and no internal study would cure it.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: gated procurement page, testimonial block

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Class IIb surgical navigation system (name not supplied)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (credentialed login, hospital procurement + clinical engineering). HWG § 11 does **not** apply. § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (copy also asserts AT/CH presence)

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 OK.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

The copy contains no breach I can identify on the material supplied. Both substantive claims are, however, unverifiable as written and rest on facts I haven't seen — which on a 27-word asset is most of the asset.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** It is a first-person account of one user's experience, presented as a quote. It does not on its face assert a general device property. But § 5(2) reaches the *geschäftliche Handlung* — the page — not only the manufacturer's own voice, and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" is expressly listed there. As the headline element of a procurement page, a bare quantified figure is read as what a buyer can expect. `[verified: UWG § 5(2) no. 1]`
**Evidence needed:** The baseline the two steps came out of (previous system? manual workflow? a prior version of your own?); whether the reduction is typical across procedure types and configurations or specific to that site's setup; whether it is documented anywhere a reader could check.
**Also engaged:**
- MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1, **if** the two-step reduction is not reproducible outside that site's workflow — then the page ascribes a property to the device it does not have. `[verified]`
- UWG § 6(2) no. 2, **if** the unstated baseline is a competitor system the German market can identify (§ 6(1) "erkennbar" does not require naming). An undefined comparator is unverifiable on the face of the copy, and that is a breach no amount of internal data cures — it is fixed by naming the comparator or dropping the comparison, not by substantiating it. If the baseline is your own earlier workflow, § 6 is not engaged at all. **Tell me which, and this moves out of "Also engaged" one way or the other.** `[verified]`

**Call:** Needs rewording + substantiation

---

**Claim:** "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Three separate factual assertions compressed into eight words — geographic scope, use status, duration — none checkable by the reader.
**Evidence needed:** Installed-base count by country as of today; whether "routine use" counts evaluation installs, pilots or research sites; the first clinical-routine go-live date; lawful market status in each of DE/AT/CH.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) (*Erfolge des Herstellers*) and UWG § 5(2) no. 3, **if** "routine use" counts pilots, evaluations or research placements as routine clinical deployment. `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 4 (*Zulassung der Waren*), **if** the device is not lawfully on the market in all three DACH countries. "DACH" includes Switzerland, which is outside the EU and outside what this skill verifies — I am not stating the Swiss requirement, only flagging that the claim asserts CH presence and something needs to confirm it. `[verify]`
- Staleness: "since 2024" is now up to two and a half years old. If the count has since shrunk, the present tense is doing work the facts don't support.

**Call:** Needs rewording + substantiation

---

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A named clinician at a named institution is the verifiable form of attribution, which is the right instinct. Two facts would change this.
**Evidence needed:** Written consent from Prof. Ellwanger and from the Klinikum for use of the institutional name; confirmation that the name and institution are as they will publish (if either was pseudonymised for this review, say so — attributing a quote to an institution that does not exist under that name is an *unwahre Angabe* under § 5(2) and, separately, destroys the verifiability that makes a named testimonial worth having).
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 3(b) reaches statements about "der für sie tätigen oder tätig gewesenen Personen" — persons working or formerly working for the manufacturer. If Prof. Ellwanger holds a consulting, advisory, speaker or research-funding relationship with you, presenting the quote with no disclosure is capable of misleading as to its independence. Disclose the relationship or confirm there is none. `[verified]`
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** Use of a professional testimonial at all
**Breach:** none — explicit non-finding
**Why:** Recording this so it doesn't get raised later. HWG § 11(1) applies only outside Fachkreise, and your audience is inside it. Independently, § 11(1) sentence 2 limits devices to nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 — so no. 2 (*Empfehlung von Fachleuten*) does not apply to a device in any audience. And no. 11 bans third-party statements only where *missbräuchlich, abstoßend oder irreführend*, not as such. `[verified: HWG § 11(1)]`
**Call:** OK

---

## Paste-ready revision

German, matching the audience:

> **Prof. Dr. med. [Vorname] Ellwanger, [Klinik/Abteilung], Universitätsklinikum Süd:**
> „Gegenüber unserem bisherigen Ablauf entfallen bei der Patientenregistrierung zwei Arbeitsschritte."
>
> Einzelerfahrung eines Anwenders. Der Umfang der Zeitersparnis ist abhängig von Eingriffsart, Workflow und Systemkonfiguration. — Prof. Ellwanger [ist bezahlter Berater der / steht in keiner geschäftlichen Beziehung zur] [Hersteller].
>
> [Produktname] ist seit [Monat/Jahr] in [Deutschland und Österreich] im klinischen Routineeinsatz; Stand [Datum]: [X] Kliniken. Die Registrierungsgenauigkeit ist vor jeder Anwendung gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung zu verifizieren.

English equivalent, if the page stays in English:

> **Prof. Dr. med. [First name] Ellwanger, [Department], Universitätsklinikum Süd:**
> "Compared with our previous workflow, patient registration lost two steps."
>
> Single-user experience. Time saved varies by procedure type, workflow and system configuration. — Prof. Ellwanger [is a paid consultant to / has no commercial relationship with] [Manufacturer].
>
> [Product] has been in clinical routine use in [Germany and Austria] since [month/year]; as of [date], [X] sites. Registration accuracy must be verified before use in accordance with the instructions for use.

Three changes carry the weight: the comparator is named in the quote itself, "every registration" becomes a bounded single-site account with the variability stated, and "DACH since 2024" becomes a dated, counted, country-specific statement a procurement reader can check.

The final sentence is my suggestion, not a finding — see the open question below before you decide whether to keep it.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "two steps out of every registration" | The baseline compared against; typicality across procedures/configurations | Clinical affairs + the site |
| Same | Whether the baseline is an identifiable competitor system | Product marketing |
| "routine use ... DACH" | Site count by country, today's date; routine vs. pilot/evaluation status | Sales ops |
| "since 2024" | First clinical-routine go-live date | Sales ops |
| DACH incl. CH | Lawful market status in AT and CH | Regulatory affairs |
| Attribution | Written consent from clinician and institution; any commercial relationship | Legal + marketing |

## Open questions I could not close

**Limb (c) — failing to inform of a likely risk.** The copy surfaces no limitation at all, and the claim is specifically about removing steps from *registration*, which is where patient-to-image accuracy is established on a navigation system. That is where I would expect a likely risk to live if one is recorded. But I have not seen your IFU, and I will not infer a risk from the device category and then flag the copy for omitting it — that produces an unfalsifiable finding. **Check this quote against what the IFU says about registration accuracy and its verification.** If the IFU records a verification step or an accuracy limitation, a pointer belongs in the copy and my suggested closing sentence covers it. # Device Claims Review: gated procurement page, testimonial + adoption line

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Surgical navigation system, Class IIb
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED** — limb (d) not assessed (see end)
**Audience:** **Fachkreise.** Credentialed login, hospital procurement and clinical engineering. HWG § 11 does **not** apply. HWG § 3 does. `[verified]`
**Markets:** DE (copy targets German market); copy also asserts AT and CH presence

## Summary

5 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 0 substantiate, 4 verify.

**No breaches identified on the material supplied.** This is short, attributed, and modest copy — it makes no outcome promise, no guarantee, and no clinical-benefit claim. The exposure here is entirely conditional on four facts I don't have. Two of those are cheap to check and one (Switzerland) is the one I'd chase first.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

Two scoping notes to preempt the usual false positives:

- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (third-party testimonials) does not apply here** — § 11 governs advertising *outside* Fachkreise only, and your audience is gated to procurement and clinical engineering. Even if the page were public, no. 11 bans testimonials only where they are *missbräuchlich, abstoßend oder irreführend*, not as such. `[verified]`
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 2 (professional endorsements) does not apply to devices at all.** § 11(1) closing sentence: *"Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend."* A review citing no. 2 against a clinician endorsement of a device is wrong. `[verified]`

---

## Findings

### 1. Reword

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** none on the face of the copy — the attribution scopes it to one named speaker's practice rather than presenting it as a general product property.
**Why:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 reaches *"von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse"* and *"wesentliche Merkmale [...] Vorteile"*. An attributed single-site experience statement is not an expected-results claim about the product. But the denominator is missing: two steps out of five is a 40% reduction, two out of twenty is 10%, and for a procurement reader weighing workflow efficiency that gap is squarely *geeignet* to move a purchasing decision under § 5(1). `[verified]`
**Evidence needed:** Total step count in the registration workflow before and after, at that site; whether the reduction is typical across installations or specific to that hospital's prior setup.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2, **if** the implied baseline ("it took two steps out of") is a competitor system the market can identify. On the copy as written the baseline reads as that hospital's own prior workflow, and § 6(1) requires the Mitbewerber to be *erkennbar* — so § 6 is probably not engaged. If your sales narrative does make the displaced system identifiable, note that an undefined comparator breaches no. 2 *on its face* and **no amount of internal data cures it** — verifiability is about what the reader can check. The fix would be to name the comparator and publish the basis, or drop the comparison. `[verified]`
**Call:** Needs rewording — add the denominator.

### 2–5. Verify

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"
**Breach:** none.
**Why:** Attributing a quote to a named clinician at a named institution is not itself a finding for a Fachkreise audience.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 3 (*unwahre oder zur Täuschung geeignete Angaben*) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1, **if** the quote is not verbatim and not authorised in writing, or if the title/affiliation is stated inaccurately. Separately: "Universitätsklinikum Süd" does not correspond to a German university hospital I can identify. If it is a pseudonym or a placeholder, the copy asserts a verifiable-looking institutional endorsement that no reader can actually check — fix it by using the real name with written consent, or by de-identifying honestly ("a university hospital in southern Germany"). Do not leave a fictional-looking specific. `[verified]`
**Call:** Verify — written consent on file, exact title, exact institution name.

**Claim:** "In routine use"
**Breach:** none.
**Why:** A true adoption statement is not misleading.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*wesentliche Merkmale [...] Verfügbarkeit*) and HWG § 3 no. 3(b) (*Erfolge des Herstellers* — the maker's track record), **if** any DACH installations are pilots, evaluation units, loaners, or sites under clinical investigation rather than routine clinical practice. "Routine use" is the load-bearing word: it asserts established adoption, and counting pilots toward it is the classic way this line goes wrong. `[verified]`
**Call:** Verify against the install base, site by site, by status.

**Claim:** "across the DACH region"
**Breach:** none.
**Why:** Geographic adoption is a factual claim, not a claim about the device.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 — *"Aussagen oder Symbole, die [...] sich auf eine Zulassung des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen"*. `[verified]` **This is the one I would check first.** DACH includes Switzerland, which is outside the EU and outside MDR. Asserting routine Swiss use implies the device holds Swiss market access, which is a separate conformity route with its own requirements. If the CH leg isn't in place, this is a § 5(2) no. 4 finding independent of whether every performance claim is accurate — and "DACH" is doing real work for a procurement reader assessing vendor stability.
The Swiss requirements themselves (Swissmedic, MedDO, authorised-representative obligations) sit outside what this skill verifies — I'm not going to state the rule. `[verify]` What I can cite is the UWG hook above. Route the Swiss status question to whoever holds your regulatory file.
**Call:** Verify — confirm Swiss market access and actual Swiss installations, or narrow to "Germany and Austria."

**Claim:** "since 2024"
**Breach:** none.
**Why:** A duration claim, plausible on its face as of today.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1, **if** "since 2024" dates from certification or first shipment rather than first routine clinical use. Those can be a year apart, and the sentence attaches the date to *routine use*. `[verified]`
**Call:** Verify against first-install records; consider stating the month.

---

## Revised copy, paste-ready

Fill the brackets from your records. Drop any bracket you cannot substantiate rather than softening it — a narrow verifiable claim is cheap to defend, a broad one is expensive even when true.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't publish as written. Both sentences are claims that need substantiation, and the testimonial has a specific German-law formality problem. None of this is fatal — it's fixable with a name, a date, a source document, and per-country numbers.

Flagging up front: this is a copy/compliance review, not legal advice. Anything you publish into the German market should get signoff from regulatory affairs and German competition counsel.

## What the gate buys you — and what it doesn't

The credentialed login matters, but less than people usually assume:

- **It does help with §11 HWG.** Hospital procurement and clinical engineering plausibly qualify as *Fachkreise* under §2 HWG (staff of institutions serving human health / persons who lawfully trade in or professionally apply medical devices). That lifts the §11 restrictions — including §11(1) no. 2, which is exactly the provision that would otherwise kill a physician testimonial. So a testimonial is permissible here in a way it wouldn't be on your public site.
- **It does nothing for MDR Art. 7.** The prohibition on misleading claims applies to all claims, gated or not, and Germany enforces it through the MPDG's penalty framework.
- **It does nothing for UWG.** §5 (misleading) and §5a (withholding material information) apply to B2B communications. In practice your realistic claimant isn't a regulator — it's a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale sending an Abmahnung. Competitors obtain credentials to gated procurement pages routinely. Treat the copy as public.
- **Copy leaks.** This language will end up in a sales deck, an RFP response, and a tender document. Once it's outside the gate, §11 is back in play. Write it so it survives that.

## Claim 1 — the testimonial

**§6 HWG formality gap.** Advertising that reproduces or refers to an expert statement must give the author's name, profession and location, state when the statement was made, and reproduce it verbatim. You currently have a surname and a partial institution. Missing: given name, medical specialty/role, location, and the date of the statement.

**The quote is in English.** If Prof. Ellwanger made this statement in German at a German university hospital, the English text is a translation, and §6's verbatim requirement points to publishing the German original. A translated paraphrase of a quantified claim is a soft spot — "took two steps out of" is loose even in English.

**"Universitätsklinikum Süd" doesn't correspond to a hospital I can identify.** If the site has been pseudonymised for privacy, say so or drop the institution entirely; a plausible-sounding but invented reference site is itself misleading, and it's the first thing a clinical engineer will try to verify. If it's real, I need the actual name.

**Consent and relationship disclosure.** You need documented written consent from the individual *and* the institution — naming a Universitätsklinikum implies institutional endorsement, and most German university hospitals have policies restricting that. If Prof. Ellwanger is a paid consultant, investigator, speaker, or KOL, disclose it. The engagement should sit under a written contract at fair market value per the MedTech Europe Code and the German BVMed/AKG codes. Given that your audience *is* the procurement decision-maker, keep §§299a/b StGB (corruption in healthcare) in view when consideration has flowed.

**A testimonial doesn't substitute for substantiation.** "Two steps out of every registration" is a quantified performance claim wearing a quote as a jacket. Under MDR Art. 7 and §3 HWG it needs evidence, and "every" asserts universality that one site's experience can't carry. Specifically:

- Two steps out of *what* baseline — your previous software version, a named competitor, or a manual workflow? If it's a competitor, §6 UWG comparative-advertising rules apply and the comparison must be objective and verifiable. If it's your own prior release, say that plainly.
- Registration workflow varies by anatomy, tracker configuration, and procedure type. Does the reduction hold across the indications in your intended purpose, or in one workflow?
- Does your CE-marked intended purpose actually cover a workflow-efficiency benefit? If the technical documentation doesn't claim step reduction, promoting it is a claim beyond the declared intended purpose.

## Claim 2 — "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024"

**Switzerland is the real risk.** Switzerland is a third country for MDR purposes. Including it requires that the device is lawfully placed on the Swiss market under the MepV — CH-REP appointed, Swissmedic obligations met. If it isn't, the sentence is both false advertising and an admission of unlawful placing on the market. Confirm this before the word "DACH" goes anywhere.

**"Across" implies breadth you should be able to count.** One site in Austria and one in Switzerland is not "across the DACH region." Replace the regional gesture with per-country installed-base numbers as of a stated date. Procurement will ask for reference sites anyway, so you lose nothing.

**"Routine use" and "since 2024" both need pinning down.** Give a month, not a year. And "routine" has to mean post-CE commercial clinical use — if the 2024 activity included clinical investigation, limited market release, or evaluation loans, calling it routine use is misleading. Also check continuity: if there's been an FSCA or field safety notice in that window, an unqualified "in routine use since" claim is exposed.

**Watch the implied safety argument.** Procurement will read "routine use since 2024" as "proven safe and reliable." MDR Art. 7(b) prohibits creating a false impression regarding safety or performance, and installed base is not clinical evidence. Keep it as a factual adoption statement and let your clinical evidence and PMCF/PSUR data carry the safety and performance claims.

## Also missing from the page

Product name, legal manufacturer, the intended purpose as declared, CE mark with notified body number, and device class. Procurement and clinical engineering need these to even start an evaluation, and §5a UWG makes withholding material information actionable. A claims-substantiation matrix — each claim mapped to its source document in the technical file — is what turns this page from a liability into an asset during a tender.

## Suggested direction

English, for your internal review:

> **[Product name]**, CE-marked Class IIb (Notified Body [NNNN]), [legal manufacturer]. Intended purpose: [as declared].
>
> Prof. Dr. med. [Given name] Ellwanger, [role, e.g. Head of the Department of Neurosurgery], [full hospital name], [city], statement of [DD.MM.YYYY]: "[German original, verbatim]"
>
> In internal usability validation ([n] users, [n] registrations, [procedure type]), registration workflow steps were reduced from [A] to [B] compared with [named baseline]. Report [ref], available on request.
>
> As of [DD.MM.YYYY], in clinical use at [n] hospitals in Germany and [n] in Austria. [Switzerland only once MepV placement is confirmed.]
>
> Disclosure: Prof. Dr. Ellwanger [is a paid consultant to / received no compensation from] [company].

The structural move is to separate the two things the original conflates: the testimonial stays a first-person account attributed to one identified clinician at one identified site, and the quantified step-reduction claim moves out of the quote and into a sentence backed by a named study with a stated method. Publish the German version as primary, since that's the market.

## What I need from you

1. Is Prof. Ellwanger a real, identifiable clinician with a signed quote release, and is the institution name real or pseudonymised?
2. Was the statement made in German, and do you have the original wording and its date?
3. Any financial or contractual relationship with Prof. Ellwanger or the institution?
4. Is the device lawfully placed on the Swiss market under the MepV?
5. What's the baseline for "two steps," and what document substantiates it?
6. Does your declared intended purpose support a workflow-efficiency claim?
7. Per-country site counts and the actual month routine clinical use began.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The gating helps a lot — but it solves the smallest of the problems here. Two of the three clauses carry claim-substantiation exposure that a credentialed login does nothing to cure, and the geography claim has a regulatory trap in it.

Quick framing on what the gate *does* buy you: HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2, which bans testimonial/expert-opinion advertising, applies only to *Publikumswerbung*. Hospital procurement and clinical engineering sit comfortably inside *Fachkreise* under HWG § 2 (staff of an institution serving human health, applying devices in the course of their profession). A real credentialed login — not a self-declaration checkbox — is the gate German courts treat as effective. So the testimonial *format* is fine. The testimonial *content* is where the problems are, and MDR Art. 7 and UWG § 5 apply identically to Fachkreise audiences.

## Blocking

**1. "Two steps out of every registration" is a quantified performance claim, not an opinion.**
Quotation marks don't convert a performance claim into a personal impression, and attributing it to a professor doesn't insulate it. "Every" makes it universal and absolute — that is the sharpest edge in the whole sentence, and it's the kind of phrasing that draws a competitor *Abmahnung*. Germany's enforcement reality is competitor litigation under UWG and the Wettbewerbszentrale, not a regulator knocking.

What you need on file before this publishes: an objective basis — a time-motion or workflow study, or the relevant section of the clinical evaluation report — showing step reduction is reproducible, not one site's experience. If the evidence is a single surgeon's impression at a single centre, the copy has to say so and drop the universal quantifier.

**2. "Across the DACH region" asserts lawful placement in Switzerland.**
Switzerland is outside the EU and the EU–CH MRA for medical devices has lapsed. Placing a Class IIb device on the Swiss market requires a Swiss Authorised Representative (CH-REP), Swiss-compliant labelling, and MepV registration obligations — all separate from your CE mark. Confirm CH-REP appointment and MepV conformity before claiming Swiss use. If Switzerland isn't properly covered, say "Germany and Austria" and the problem disappears.

**3. Named KOL requires documented consent and relationship disclosure.**
Three separate things to secure:
- Written consent from Prof. Ellwanger for this exact wording, plus separate institutional sign-off from the Universitätsklinikum for use of its name — hospitals typically govern this tightly.
- Disclosure of any financial relationship: consulting fees, research funding, honoraria, discounted equipment. Undisclosed paid endorsement is *Schleichwerbung* and engages UWG § 5a on withholding material information. If you're a MedTech Europe member, its Code of Ethical Business Practice points the same way.
- Be aware the professor has their own exposure under (Muster-)Berufsordnung § 27 on physicians lending their name to product advertising. Not your legal risk directly, but it's the reason hospitals pull endorsements late, and it's worth raising with them before you build a campaign on it.

## Should fix

**4. "Routine use" needs a denominator.** "Across the DACH region" implies breadth. If it's four hospitals, that's misleading under MDR Art. 7 and UWG § 5. Replace with a countable fact: "In clinical use at *N* centres in Germany and Austria since *[month]* 2024."

**5. Check "since 2024" against the certificate.** Verify the date matches first placing on market for *this* configuration under the current Class IIb certificate. If the 2024 use was a prior version, or under an investigational arrangement, the claim doesn't hold.

**6. Gate hygiene — the gate only protects what's behind it.** Confirm: the page is `noindex`, there's no ungated teaser or search snippet carrying the quote, and there's no downloadable PDF or social card that escapes the login. Any fragment that surfaces publicly becomes Publikumswerbung and HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 bites on the testimonial after all. Also confirm credentialing verifies professional status at signup rather than taking a tickbox.

**7. Keep German as the master version.** For a German market this will publish in German; the quote was presumably given in German. Archive the original German wording with the signed approval so the English isn't the authority on what was said.

## Suggested revision

Assuming substantiation exists, slots in brackets:

> Prof. Ellwanger, Universitätsklinikum Süd: "In unserem Ablauf entfielen damit zwei Schritte der Registrierungssequenz."
>
> Einzelbeobachtung aus dem klinischen Routinebetrieb; die Ergebnisse hängen von Arbeitsablauf und Falltyp ab. Prof. Ellwanger erhält Beraterhonorare von [Unternehmen].
>
> Seit [Monat] 2024 im klinischen Einsatz an [N] Zentren in Deutschland und Österreich.

This keeps the quote's substance, drops "every," marks it as a single-site observation, discloses the relationship, and makes the footprint countable.

If the workflow study does exist and supports a general claim, you can go further and state the step reduction as a substantiated product claim in your own voice — which is stronger copy than a testimonial anyway, and easier to defend.

One caveat: this is a claims-review read, not regulatory affairs sign-off. Items 1, 2 and 3 should go to your RA/legal function with the substantiation file attached before publication.
