graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The gating is doing real legal work here — both claims are far riskier off-gate than on it — but neither claim is safe as written. Claim 1 is an unsubstantiated quantified performance claim in testimonial form; Claim 2 is a scope claim that likely overstates geography and regulatory status. I'm reviewing as a reg/marketing reviewer, not as your counsel; the German-law points should be confirmed by your HWG/UWG advisor before publication.

## The gate: what it buys you, and what it doesn't

Hospital procurement and clinical engineering staff acting for a Klinikum almost certainly fall inside **Fachkreise** under HWG §2 (Einrichtungen, die der Gesundheit von Menschen dienen; persons who apply devices in their professional practice). That matters because a named professor's endorsement is the kind of content HWG §11 Abs. 1 restricts **outside** Fachkreise — notably Nr. 1 (Gutachten/Zeugnisse) and Nr. 2 (Angaben, dass das Mittel ärztlich empfohlen oder geprüft ist). Inside Fachkreise, §11 Abs. 1 doesn't apply. HWG §3 (Irreführung), UWG §§5, 5a, and MDR Art. 7 apply regardless of audience.

Two conditions on that:

- **The gate must be real.** Credentialed login with verified professional identity is defensible; a self-declaration checkbox is the pattern German courts have found insufficient. Confirm the credential check actually verifies role, and that procurement/clinical-engineering roles are within the accepted categories.
- **The copy must not leak.** The moment this quote appears in a press release, LinkedIn post, trade-show handout, sales PDF, or the page's meta description/SEO snippet, it's Publikumswerbung and §11 Abs. 1 bites. Tag this copy block as gate-only in your asset system. Same applies to any accompanying photo of Prof. Ellwanger in scrubs or at work — §11 Abs. 1 Nr. 4.

## Claim 1 — the testimonial

"It took two steps out of every registration."

- **No comparator.** Two steps out of *what* — your previous software version, manual registration, a named competitor? An unstated baseline is the classic Irreführung finding under HWG §3 / UWG §5. If the implicit baseline is an identifiable competitor, UWG §6 kicks in and the comparison must be objective and verifiable.
- **"Every registration" is an absolute claim.** It asserts universality. One professor's impression at one site cannot support it. Either substantiate it as a product characteristic (workflow step count is verifiable from the IFU — this may be your easiest fix) or drop the universality.
- **Attribution doesn't transfer liability.** Under MDR Art. 7 the claim is yours once you publish it, quotation marks or not.
- **IFU consistency is the safety-critical issue.** For a Class IIb navigation system, if the copy implies steps have been removed from registration but the IFU still requires them — particularly any accuracy-verification step — you're promoting a workflow that deviates from the intended use. Have the copy checked against the current IFU step-by-step.
- **Disclosure.** If Prof. Ellwanger is a paid consultant, investigator, or has any financial relationship, undisclosed material connection is Schleichwerbung under UWG §5a and breaches the MedTech Europe Code / BVMed Kodex. Disclose it on the page.
- **Consent, two layers.** Written release from Prof. Ellwanger *and* institutional sign-off from the Klinikum for use of its name — public hospitals have Neutralitätspflicht constraints and usually refuse implied product endorsement.
- **The physician's own exposure.** MBO-Ä §27 restricts physicians from lending their name and professional standing to product advertising. Flag this to him before publication; it's his risk but it can rebound on you via UWG §3a.
- **Verify the institution exists as named.** "Universitätsklinikum Süd" reads like a placeholder or anonymisation. A composite or pseudonymous attribution presented as a real named source is straightforwardly misleading — resolve this before anything else.
- **Language.** German-market page, and this quote is evidently translated. Publish the German original verbatim; a paraphrase that tightens the claim is a real hazard.

## Claim 2 — "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024"

- **"Across the DACH region"** implies all three countries and meaningful breadth. If the installed base is a handful of German sites, it fails. Replace with countable facts: number of sites, countries, procedure volume.
- **Switzerland is a separate regulatory market.** Post-MRA, CH requires a Swiss Authorized Representative, Swiss-conformant labelling, and Swissmedic registration; advertising claims fall under MepV. If you aren't CH-compliant, saying the device is in routine use there is both a false claim and an admission.
- **"Routine use" has clinical meaning.** If 2024 usage included clinical investigation, limited market release, or evaluation installs, "routine" is false. Check what fraction of that use was investigational.
- **"Since 2024" must track the certificate.** Confirm the CE certificate date under MDR for *this* configuration. If the 2024 deployments ran an earlier version or a different regulatory basis, the claim silently misattributes history to the current product.

## Substantiation to file before publication

Build a claims-substantiation matrix in the technical documentation (MDR Art. 7): IFU step-count comparison old vs. new; the underlying workflow/time-motion data with defined comparator and n; signed testimonial release and institutional consent; financial-relationship disclosure record; installed-base list by country with go-live dates and regulatory basis; CE certificate reference; German source text of the quote.

## Suggested safer version

> "Reduces patient-to-image registration from [N] to [N−2] steps compared with [named prior version / specified manual workflow]" — verifiable from the IFU, no testimonial dependency, explicit comparator.
>
> "In clinical use at [N] hospitals in Germany and Austria since [Month] 2024" — countable, geographically honest, no "routine" overreach. Add Switzerland only once CH-REP and registration are in place.

If you want to keep the human voice, keep the quote but strip the quantified claim from it and let it carry the qualitative experience, with the numbers made separately and substantiated: *"Prof. Ellwanger, Universitätsklinikum [real name] — [qualitative quote]. Prof. Ellwanger is a paid consultant to [company]."*

The single item to resolve first: whether "Universitätsklinikum Süd" is a real, consenting institution. Everything else is fixable copy; that one is either fine or fatal.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: consumer web page, blood-pressure monitor

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor, Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum (ungated public consumer page) — HWG § 11 applies, nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only
**Markets:** DE (EU rules apply cumulatively)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No, rewrite needed.**

The fear framing is the serious one. "Don't gamble with your heart" is close to the textbook shape of HWG § 11(1) no. 7, and § 11 applies in full here because the page is ungated consumer-facing. It cannot be fixed with evidence — it has to come out.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart, check your pressure daily."
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`
**Why:** The sentence works by suggesting that health is at risk if the device is *not* used — the operative words are "dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** ... beeinträchtigt ... werden könnte". "Gamble with your heart" is a direct fear-of-not-using construction, and the second half supplies the implied improvement-by-use half of the same provision.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. § 11 no. 7 prohibits the framing, not an unsubstantiated fact.
**Call:** Cut

**Claim:** same sentence, second issue
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** Read as one unit, the copy implies that daily measurement protects the heart — "creating a false impression regarding treatment". A blood-pressure monitor measures; it does not reduce cardiac risk. The protective outcome is implied, never stated, which is exactly what limb (b) reaches.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — the implication is structural. Narrowing the claim to what the device does (measurement) removes it.
**Call:** Cut

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A measurement-frequency instruction is a clinical instruction. Whether it is defensible depends entirely on what the IFU and the assessed intended purpose say about measurement regimen.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") `[verified]`, if the intended purpose or IFU does not support unsupervised daily self-measurement as the recommended use pattern. If it does not, this is intended-purpose drift and evidence will not cure it — the claim has to narrow.
**Call:** Verify — this is the specific line to test against the intended purpose when you have it.

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Worth being explicit about what is *not* wrong here, because this is commonly over-flagged: HWG § 11(1) no. 2 (professional endorsements) does **not** apply to medical devices — the closing sentence of § 11(1) limits devices to nos. 7–9, 11 and 12 `[verified]`. A clinician endorsement of a device is not per se prohibited. No. 11 reaches third-party statements only "in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise", and nothing in the quoted words is abusive or repulsive on its face.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 and UWG § 5(1) `[verified]`, if Prof. Schmidt has a paid or other commercial relationship with the manufacturer that the page does not disclose — an undisclosed material connection is the route by which an otherwise lawful testimonial becomes *irreführend*.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]`, on the same facts: statements "im Zusammenhang mit direktem oder indirektem Sponsoring".
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) and UWG § 5(2) no. 3 `[verified]`, if the title "Professor" or the specialty "cardiologist" is not accurate and current, or if the person is not identifiable. A surname with no first name, no institution and no country is not checkable by a reader.
**Evidence needed:** written consent on file; confirmation of title, specialty and institution; disclosure of any fee, equity, advisory role or research funding.
**Call:** Verify — usable if the three items above hold and the relationship is disclosed on the page.

---

**On limb (c) — I am not raising it.** The copy surfaces no limitation at all, and for a consumer BP monitor there is an obvious candidate (readings need clinical interpretation; self-measurement is not a diagnosis). But I have not seen your IFU, and inferring a "likely risk" from the device category and then flagging the copy for omitting it would be an unfalsifiable finding. Check the copy against the IFU's warnings and limitations section; if a likely risk is recorded there, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix.

## Replacement copy, paste-ready

Option A — drop the endorsement:

> Measure your blood pressure at home in about a minute. Talk to your doctor about your readings and how often to measure.

Option B — keep the endorsement, disclosed and identifiable:

> Measure your blood pressure at home in about a minute. Talk to your doctor about your readings and how often to measure.
>
> Recommended by Prof. Dr. [full name], Cardiologist, [institution]. [Paid advisor to / compensated by] [company name].

German rendering of Option A, for the live page:

> Messen Sie Ihren Blutdruck zu Hause in etwa einer Minute. Besprechen Sie Ihre Messwerte und die Häufigkeit der Messungen mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.

Treat the German as a rendering of the cleared English, not as separately reviewed — the final German wording should get its own pass, since § 11 no. 7 turns on the connotation of the actual German words.

What the rewrite does: removes the risk-if-you-don't-use framing entirely, states only what the device does (measures), and routes the frequency question to a clinician rather than asserting a regimen the technical file may not support.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Intended purpose | The intended purpose verbatim from the DoC / technical documentation | RA/QA |
| "check your pressure daily" | IFU statement on measurement frequency and self-measurement | RA/QA |
| Any risk omission | IFU warnings/limitations section | RA/QA |
| "Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" | Written consent; verified title, specialty, institution | Marketing / legal |
| Endorsement disclosure | Any fee, advisory, equity or funding relationship | Finance / legal |

## Limb (d)

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, and here it bears directly on "check your pressure daily". Paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c) plus the German overlay.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11, and the device scoping sentence — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6 — not engaged; the copy makes no comparison.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: consumer web page copy (2 sentences)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device / IVD:** Home blood-pressure monitor, Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum (ungated public consumer page) → HWG § 11(1) applies, nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only
**Markets:** DE (+ EU)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.**

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed. One clause has to be cut rather than softened: it is a fear-of-not-using appeal, which is a breach on its face and cannot be cured by evidence.

One thing the copy is **not** doing wrong, because it is the most common false positive here: HWG § 11(1) **no. 2** (recommendations by health professionals) does **not** apply to medical devices — the closing sentence of § 11(1) limits devices to nos. 7 to 9, 11 and 12 `[verified]`. A cardiologist endorsement is therefore **not** prohibited per se. It is tested under no. 11, which bites only where the third-party statement is missbräuchlich, abstoßend or irreführend.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`; HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** No. 7 prohibits copy "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** [...] beeinträchtigt [...] werden könnte" — the clause's entire function is to say that not measuring puts your heart at risk. Coupled with the imperative to measure, it also creates a false impression of a protective/therapeutic effect (Art. 7(b); § 3 no. 1 "Wirkungen beigelegt werden, die sie nicht haben"): a BP monitor measures, it does not reduce cardiac risk.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Even a monitor with outstanding accuracy data does not protect a heart, and no. 7 targets the framing, not the truth of an underlying fact.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** Replace the risk framing with a factual statement of what the device does — see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`, second limb, as it currently stands — in this sentence the measurement instruction carries the "Gesundheit durch die Verwendung verbessert" implication rather than standing as a neutral usage statement.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") `[verified]`, if the assessed intended purpose and the IFU do not support an unqualified daily self-measurement regimen for the general public. Measurement frequency is normally a clinical decision; copy that sets it for every reader may suggest a use, and a user population, beyond what the conformity assessment covered. I cannot resolve this without the intended purpose.
**Evidence needed:** Intended purpose as assessed, plus the IFU's measurement-frequency text. A (d) problem is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment, not by data.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** Attribute the frequency to the IFU or to the user's doctor rather than asserting it — "measure as often as your doctor recommends" / "as described in the instructions for use".

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied. A professional recommendation is lawful for a device (no. 2 does not apply); as written it asserts nothing I can test against the statute.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — if the recommendation is not genuine, not current, not given for this device, or is presented in a way that misleads (irreführend).
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — unwahre oder zur Täuschung geeignete Angaben "über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung [...] der für sie tätigen [...] Personen", if Prof. Schmidt acts or has acted for the manufacturer (advisory board, paid spokesperson, consultancy) and the title, specialty or standing is overstated.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 3 `[verified]` — "Person, Eigenschaften [...] Befähigung, Status, Zulassung, [...] Auszeichnungen", same condition.
- The undisclosed-payment question sits under no. 11 and § 5, **not** under § 11(1) no. 9: on an own-brand product page the promotional purpose is plainly recognisable, so no. 9 does not bite.

**Evidence needed:** Written, dated consent to be named; confirmation the title "Professor" and the Facharzt für Kardiologie qualification are current and correctly stated; confirmation the recommendation covers *this* device; and the nature of any financial or contractual relationship.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** Identify the person fully and disclose any relationship — a bare surname plus a title is the shape that later reads as irreführend.

---

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU. For this device category the candidate is usually that readings require clinical interpretation and do not replace medical assessment — but I am not flagging (c) on that basis, because I would be inferring the risk from the product category rather than reading it in your documentation. Confirm from the IFU and I will place it.

### Not engaged

- **UWG § 6** — no comparison, direct or indirect. No competitor is made erkennbar.
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 4** — no CE, class, or notified-body claim in the copy.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)/(b)** — no guarantee of success and no "no side effects" claim.
- **HWG § 3a** — Arzneimittel only; never applies to a device.

## Paste-ready revised copy

Reviewed text was English; both versions below carry the same claim structure.

> **EN:** "Clinically validated home blood-pressure measurement, recommended by Prof. Dr. [full name], Facharzt für Kardiologie, [institution]. Measure as often as your doctor advises and share your readings at your next appointment. Readings do not replace medical assessment. Please read the instructions for use."

> **DE:** "Klinisch validierte Blutdruckmessung für zuhause — empfohlen von Prof. Dr. [vollständiger Name], Facharzt für Kardiologie, [Institution]. Messen Sie so häufig, wie es Ihre Ärztin oder Ihr Arzt empfiehlt, und besprechen Sie Ihre Werte beim nächsten Termin. Die Messwerte ersetzen keine ärztliche Beurteilung. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung."

Two conditions on using it: drop "clinically validated" unless you hold validation data for this device (otherwise MDR Art. 7(a), UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "Tests"), and add a relationship disclosure next to the name if one exists.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "check your pressure daily" | Intended purpose as assessed + IFU measurement-frequency text | RA / technical documentation owner |
| Prof. Schmidt recommendation | Dated written consent, current title and Facharzt qualification, device covered, any financial relationship | Marketing / legal |
| "clinically validated" (if used) | Validation or clinical-evaluation report for this device | RA / clinical |
| Limb (c) | Whether the IFU records a likely risk for in-line-with-purpose use | RA |

## Limb (d)

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file |
|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(b), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]` |
| HWG § 3 no. 1, no. 3(b) | `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` |
| HWG § 11(1) no. 7, no. 9, no. 11, and the devices scoping sentence | `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4; § 6(1) | `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` |

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: consumer web page headline

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Class IIa home blood-pressure monitor
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum (ungated public consumer page) — HWG § 11(1) applies, nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only
**Markets:** EU + DE

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 substantiate, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed. The second sentence carries a breach on the face of the copy that evidence cannot cure.

One scoping point first, because it is the most common false positive in this exact scenario: **HWG § 11(1) no. 2** (endorsements by members of the healing professions) does **not** apply to medical devices. The closing sentence of § 11(1) limits device applicability to nos. 7 to 9, 11 and 12 `[verified]`. A clinician endorsement of a device is therefore **not** prohibited as such — it is tested under no. 11, which bites only where the third-party statement is missbräuchlich, abstoßend or irreführend. If anyone has told you this line is per se unlawful under § 11, that is wrong on the statute text.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart, check your pressure daily."
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits Werbeaussagen "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** [...] beeinträchtigt oder durch die **Verwendung verbessert** werden könnte". "Don't gamble with your heart" says exactly that — not checking puts your heart at risk — and the imperative that follows supplies the improvement-by-use half. Separately, Art. 7(b): the framing leaves the impression that the act of measuring protects cardiac health, which is an outcome a measurement-only device does not deliver; the device produces a reading, not a reduction in cardiac risk.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. § 11(1) no. 7 targets the rhetorical shape, not the truth of the underlying proposition. Even if daily home measurement is clinically beneficial, the fear framing is the problem.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse"), and UWG generally as the enforcement route by which an HWG breach arrives as an Abmahnung.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** see rewrite below.

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** not assessed for MDR Art. 7(d) — intended purpose not supplied
**Why:** Prescribing a measurement frequency is a usage instruction, not a product description. Whether a self-directed daily regimen sits inside the assessed intended purpose, and whether it matches the measurement protocol in the IFU, is the exact question limb (d) asks. A true and clinically sensible frequency still breaches (d) if the conformity assessment covered something narrower.
**Evidence needed:** the intended purpose as assessed, plus the IFU measurement protocol. If they diverge from "daily", the cure is narrowing the claim or extending the assessment — not data.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit"), the UWG mirror of intended-purpose drift, if the regimen is outside assessed use.
**Call:** Needs rewording — point to the IFU rather than setting a frequency in marketing copy.

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** For devices, third-party statements are governed by HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]`, which prohibits them only "wenn diese in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise erfolgen". A named clinician's recommendation, accurately attributed and disclosed, does not meet that threshold on its face. § 11(1) no. 2 is not available against a device.
**Evidence needed:** written consent and the actual wording of the recommendation; confirmation that the Professor title and the cardiology qualification are held as stated; the nature of any commercial or employment relationship with the manufacturer.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]`, if the relationship is undisclosed, the attribution is loose ("recommended" doing work an actual statement does not support), or the endorsement reaches beyond the assessed intended purpose — a testimonial is a common vector for limb (d) drift.
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]`, if Schmidt is or was working for the manufacturer and the stated credentials overstate "Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung".
- UWG § 5(2) no. 3 `[verified]`, if the endorsement is presented so as to imply an institutional or professional status the company does not hold.
- HWG § 11(1) no. 9 `[verified]`, not engaged on a product page where the promotional purpose is obvious; it would engage if this line is reused in editorial or native placements.

**Call:** Verify — retain the line, subject to the checks above and an affiliation disclosure where one exists.

---

### Open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation and no pointer to clinical interpretation of readings. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — so I am **not** raising MDR Art. 7(c). Naming a risk I inferred from the device category and then flagging the copy for omitting it would be unfalsifiable. Worth checking against the IFU: if it records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose (for example any contraindication, or a requirement that readings be interpreted by a clinician), (c) becomes live and an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix.

## Paste-ready rewrite

English, matching the submitted language:

> **Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist.\*** Measure your blood pressure at home, following the measurement protocol in the instructions for use, and discuss your readings with your doctor.
>
> \*Prof. Schmidt is a paid advisor to [company]. *(Include only if true; delete if there is no relationship.)*

German, for the DE-market page:

> **Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. Schmidt, Kardiologe.\*** Messen Sie Ihren Blutdruck zu Hause gemäß der Messanleitung in der Gebrauchsanweisung und besprechen Sie Ihre Werte mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.
>
> \*Prof. Dr. Schmidt ist bezahlter Berater von [Unternehmen].

What changed and why: the fear frame is gone (§ 11(1) no. 7); "daily" is replaced by a pointer to the IFU protocol, which removes the Art. 7(d) exposure without weakening the call to action; the clinician-discussion clause carries the message the fear line was doing, in a form that does not assert health impairment from non-use.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "check your pressure daily" | Intended purpose exactly as assessed; IFU measurement protocol | RA/QA — technical documentation, DoC |
| Endorsement | Signed consent, verbatim recommendation, scope of what was endorsed | Marketing / Prof. Schmidt |
| Endorsement | Title and specialty verification; any consultancy, employment or payment relationship | Legal / HR / Marketing |
| Omission check | Whether the IFU records a likely risk or interpretation requirement | RA/QA — IFU |

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Status | Reference file |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(b), (c), (d) | `[verified]` | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| HWG § 3 no. 3(b) | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 9, 11 | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 11(1) closing sentence (device scoping) | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| UWG § 5(2) nos. 1, 3 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |

## To close out limb (d)

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, and here it bears directly on both the "daily" frequency and the scope of what Prof. Schmidt is presented as endorsing. Paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

## Verdict

Both sentences are non-compliant for an ungated German consumer page. I'd treat this as blocking, not fixable by softening the wording — the endorsement has to come out entirely and the fear framing has to be replaced.

Standard caveat: this is a compliance read, not legal advice. Have your German regulatory counsel confirm the paragraph numbering before you rely on it.

## Blocking issue 1 — "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist"

The Heilmittelwerbegesetz (HWG) applies to medical devices (§ 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG, which references Art. 2 Nr. 1 MDR). For advertising directed at the public — *Publikumswerbung*, which an ungated web page is — § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 HWG prohibits advertising with statements that the product is professionally recommended, tested, or used, or that reference a recommendation by scientists or persons working in healthcare. A named cardiologist's recommendation is the textbook case.

Notes on scope:

- It does not matter whether the recommendation is true, whether Prof. Schmidt is paid, or whether you add a disclosure. The prohibition is per se for the consumer channel.
- If there's an accompanying photo of the professor in a white coat or clinical setting, that's a separate hit under § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 4 HWG (depiction of healthcare professionals in professional dress / practising their occupation).
- The endorsing physician has their own exposure under § 27 MBO-Ä (berufswidrige Werbung — physicians may not lend their name to product advertising), so this is a risk you're creating for them too.
- If "Professor Schmidt" is a composite or illustrative figure rather than a real consenting person, add misleading advertising under § 5 UWG and MDR Art. 7 to the list. If real, you need documented written consent for name use plus substantiation of the recommendation on file.

**Where it *can* live:** a genuinely gated HCP area addressed to *Fachkreise* (§ 2 HWG) is outside § 11's reach. § 3 HWG and the UWG still apply there, as does the physician's professional-code problem. Gating means real access control, not a "I am a healthcare professional" checkbox.

## Blocking issue 2 — "Don't gamble with your heart"

Two separate problems in six words.

**Fear-based appeal.** § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 7 HWG prohibits consumer advertising with statements apt to induce or exploit anxiety. "Don't gamble with your heart" works precisely by suggesting that not using the product puts your heart at risk. This is one of the more reliably enforced provisions.

**Claim beyond intended purpose.** The device's intended purpose is non-invasive measurement of blood pressure. The copy implies cardiac protection — that using it safeguards your heart. Measuring is not treating, and a monitor prevents nothing on its own. That's a misleading claim under MDR Art. 7 (text creating a false impression regarding functions the device does not have) and § 3 HWG, and any promotional claim has to be consistent with the intended purpose and supported by your clinical evaluation.

## Secondary issue — "check your pressure daily"

This is a clinical recommendation on measurement frequency, issued by the manufacturer to consumers. Three things to resolve:

1. It must match your IFU. If the IFU doesn't recommend daily measurement, the web page contradicts the accompanying documentation.
2. It isn't what the guidelines say. ESH/ESC home-monitoring guidance centres on structured 7-day schedules (duplicate morning and evening readings, typically around consultations or during titration), not indefinite daily self-measurement. Routine daily measurement in unselected consumers is associated with anxiety and over-consultation.
3. Telling patients how often to measure, rather than deferring to their physician, is you giving medical advice. Refer the frequency decision to the treating physician.

## Suggested rewrite

Substance first — final copy needs to be in German for this market, so treat the English as a brief for the translator, and have the German reviewed rather than the English.

> **Klinisch validiert.** Die Messgenauigkeit ist nach ISO 81060‑2 geprüft.
>
> **Regelmäßig messen, Werte im Blick behalten.** Wie oft Sie zu Hause messen sollten, besprechen Sie am besten mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.

(EN gloss: "Clinically validated — measurement accuracy tested to ISO 81060‑2." / "Measure regularly, keep track of your values. How often you should measure at home is best discussed with your doctor.")

This swaps a prohibited personal endorsement for an objective, product-level, substantiable fact, and swaps the fear appeal for a neutral benefit statement that defers frequency to the clinician.

Only use the ISO 81060‑2 line if you actually hold the validation report — clinical-validation claims are substantiation-bearing. A Deutsche Hochdruckliga *Prüfsiegel*, if you hold one, is widely used in German consumer BP-monitor advertising; I'd still run it past counsel, since § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 reaches "professionally tested" and the permissibility rests on it being an objective institutional test mark rather than a personal recommendation.

## Before publishing

- Sweep the rest of the page and any linked assets for the same two patterns — expert endorsements and "what if you don't" framing tend to recur in headline, meta description, and social cards.
- Check whether Prof. Schmidt appears in imagery, video, or structured data anywhere else in the campaign.
- Confirm all on-page claims trace to the clinical evaluation and the IFU.

Enforcement risk here is real and cheap to trigger: HWG breaches in consumer advertising are routinely pursued by competitors and by bodies like the Wettbewerbszentrale and VSW via *Abmahnung*, and a named-physician endorsement on an open web page is about as visible as it gets.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish as written

Both halves of this sentence carry real exposure — one as a misleading endorsement, one as an unsupported health-outcome claim that exceeds the device's intended purpose. For a Class IIa device on an ungated German consumer page, you are in the strictest advertising regime available: lay audience (*Werbung außerhalb der Fachkreise*), full MDR Art. 7 exposure, and a very active *Abmahnung* market (Wettbewerbszentrale, Verband Sozialer Wettbewerb).

---

### 1. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — high risk

**Unverifiable authority cue.** No full name, no title, no institution, no specialty board, no date, no scope of what was recommended. As written this functions as a generic "a professor says so" signal, which is misleading under **UWG § 5** and **MDR Art. 7** (false impression as to the device's properties). This is the single most Abmahnung-prone element here.

**An individual opinion is not clinical evidence.** Under MDR, performance claims must trace to your clinical evaluation / validation data (for a BP monitor: **ISO 81060-2** validation, ideally an ESH-listed validation). A named cardiologist's endorsement substantiates nothing and cannot stand in for that file.

**Undisclosed material connection.** If Prof. Schmidt is paid, an advisory-board member, an investigator, or holds equity, that must be disclosed — **UWG § 5a Abs. 4** plus UWG Anhang Nr. 11 (paid content presented as editorial/independent).

**German physician professional law.** German physicians are restricted from lending their name and professional title to commercial product advertising (Musterberufsordnung / state *Berufsordnungen* — the *Werbeverbot* provisions around MBO-Ä §§ 27, 34). If the endorsement breaches the doctor's professional code, a competitor can attack *you* via **UWG § 3a**. Verify the exact provisions of the applicable *Landesärztekammer* Berufsordnung with counsel.

**HWG.** The Heilmittelwerbegesetz applies to medical device advertising. Historic § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 (a flat ban on "ärztlich empfohlen" in lay advertising) was repealed in the 2012 reform, so a physician recommendation is no longer *per se* prohibited — but the surviving provisions on expert opinions/certificates and on third-party statements (abusive, repellent, or misleading) still bite, and some of those numbers carry device-specific carve-outs. **Have counsel confirm the current numbering and the device carve-outs before you rely on any of it** — I'd flag the substance as settled and the citations as needing verification.

**If imagery accompanies this:** a white coat, stethoscope, or clinical setting triggers the separate HWG ban on depicting healthcare professionals in professional dress or practising. Drop it.

### 2. "Don't gamble with your heart" — high risk

A fear appeal that implies non-use of the device endangers your heart, and that daily use prevents cardiac events. Two distinct problems:

- **MDR Art. 7(a), (b) and (d):** it ascribes a preventive/protective function the device does not have. The intended purpose is *measuring* blood pressure, not reducing cardiovascular risk. Implying outcome benefit is off-label promotion.
- **German healthcare-advertising law restricts fear-inducing claims and claims that health will suffer without the product**, on top of general **UWG § 5** misleadingness and **§ 4a** (undue influence / exploiting vulnerability). Again: substance is clear, exact HWG subsection to be confirmed by counsel.

There is no version of this line I'd try to save. Cut it.

### 3. "check your pressure daily" — medium/high risk

This is a clinical dosing instruction, and it is inconsistent with guideline practice. ESH 2023 and German guidance (DEGAM, Deutsche Hochdruckliga) recommend a **structured 7-day schedule — morning and evening, two readings each** — around diagnosis and treatment changes, not indefinite daily measurement for every user. Two consequences:

- If your IFU doesn't specify daily measurement, advertising it is **off-label promotion (MDR Art. 7(d))**. Check the IFU wording first.
- Unstructured daily measurement drives measurement anxiety and self-titration. There's also an **MDR Art. 7(c)** angle: failing to inform the user of a likely risk of normal use.

### 4. Cross-cutting gaps

- **Language.** German market, German consumers — publish in German. Device information must be in German under MDR Annex I §23 / MPDG; keep marketing consistent with that.
- **No intended purpose stated.** Add a plain statement of what the device does and that it's a medical device.
- **No "consult your doctor" / no-self-diagnosis line.** Expected for a diagnostic-adjacent consumer device.
- **Do not** add the medicines boilerplate ("Zu Risiken und Nebenwirkungen…") — that's Arzneimittel-only and wrong here.
- **Claims substantiation matrix.** Every surviving claim needs a row linking it to the clinical evaluation, ISO 81060-2 validation report, or IFU. Build it before launch; it's what you'll be asked for.

---

## Suggested rewrite (German, compliant shape)

> **Blutdruck zuhause messen — klinisch validiert.**
> [Produktname] ist ein Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa zur Messung von Blutdruck und Puls am Oberarm. Die Messgenauigkeit ist nach ISO 81060-2 klinisch validiert.
> Wie oft und zu welchen Zeiten Sie messen sollten, besprechen Sie mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt. Einzelne Messwerte ersetzen keine ärztliche Diagnose.
> Gebrauchsanweisung beachten.

English equivalent for your review file: *"Measure your blood pressure at home. [Product] is a Class IIa medical device for measuring blood pressure and pulse at the upper arm, with accuracy clinically validated to ISO 81060-2. Talk to your doctor about how often and when to measure. Individual readings do not replace a medical diagnosis. Follow the instructions for use."*

**If you want to keep the expert:** reposition from endorsement to disclosed advisory involvement — *"Wissenschaftliche Beratung: Prof. Dr. med. [Vollständiger Name], Facharzt für Kardiologie, [Klinik/Institution] — entgeltliche Beratungstätigkeit für [Hersteller]"* — with the physician's written consent, and run it past the applicable Berufsordnung. Note this still doesn't substantiate any performance claim; it's transparency, not evidence.

---

**Before launch:** confirm the daily-measurement wording against your actual IFU, and get the HWG subsection numbers and the Berufsordnung question verified by German regulatory counsel. I've stated the substantive prohibitions with confidence; the specific HWG numbering has moved twice since 2012 and I'd rather you check it than cite it from me.

## Verdict: don't publish. Both halves of this line are problems under German law.

This is a Class IIa device advertised to the general public in Germany, so the **Heilmittelwerbegesetz (HWG)** applies alongside **MDR Art. 7**. (Not legal advice — route the final text through your regulatory affairs / competition-law counsel.)

---

### 1. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — hard block

**§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 2 HWG** prohibits advertising *außerhalb der Fachkreise* (i.e. to the public) with statements that a product is "ärztlich … oder anderweitig fachlich empfohlen oder geprüft." A named cardiologist's recommendation is the textbook case. There's no fix by rewording — the endorsement itself has to go from public-facing copy.

Related exposure on the same line:
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 1 HWG** if you support it with expert opinions, certificates, or references to publications.
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 4 HWG** if any accompanying image shows a person in professional clothing or performing medical activity.
- **UWG § 5a Abs. 4** if the endorsement is paid and the commercial relationship isn't disclosed — and **§ 5** if "Professor Schmidt" is a placeholder/composite rather than a real, consenting person who actually said this. Right now the name reads like a stand-in; a fabricated expert is straightforward misleading advertising.

An expert endorsement can live in **HCP-facing (Fachkreise) material behind proper gating**, with documented consent and disclosed relationship. It cannot live on an ungated consumer page.

### 2. "Don't gamble with your heart" — fear-based appeal

This works by implying that not using the device endangers your health. That's the pattern **§ 11 Abs. 1 HWG** targets with its Angstwerbung provision (I'd have counsel confirm the exact current numbering — that subsection was reworked in the 2012 amendment and its application to devices vs. medicinal products is worth checking). Independently, **MDR Art. 7** prohibits claims that mislead the user about the device's function or that exploit risk perception. Swap the coercion for a benefit statement.

### 3. "Check your pressure daily" — clinical claim outside the intended purpose

Two separate issues:

- **Scope:** this is a usage recommendation. It must match the intended purpose in your technical documentation and the IFU. If the IFU doesn't specify daily measurement, the ad is claiming something the registered device documentation doesn't support (**MDR Art. 7**, and **§ 3a HWG** for advertising outside the approved intended purpose).
- **Substance:** ESH/ESC guidance on home measurement generally describes structured schedules — duplicate morning and evening readings over ~3–7 days around a clinical decision point — not indefinite daily self-measurement by the general public. Telling untriaged consumers to measure daily is an unsubstantiated clinical instruction and can drive white-coat anxiety and over-consultation.

### 4. Missing / procedural

- **Language:** consumer-facing copy for the German market must be in German.
- **Medizinprodukt notice:** German consumer advertising for medical devices conventionally carries a mandatory-style hint ("Dies ist ein Medizinprodukt. Zu Risiken und Nebenwirkungen lesen Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung…"). Confirm the current statutory basis and exact wording with counsel — I don't want to give you a citation I'm not certain of — but assume you need it.
- **Claim substantiation file:** every retained claim needs a traceable evidence record under MDR Art. 7.

---

### Suggested replacement

**DE:**
> Blutdruck zuverlässig zu Hause messen — klinisch validiert nach [Protokoll/Norm].
> Regelmäßige Selbstmessung hilft Ihnen, Ihre Werte zwischen den Arztterminen im Blick zu behalten. Wie häufig Sie messen sollten, besprechen Sie bitte mit Ihrer Arztpraxis.
>
> [Produktname] ist ein Medizinprodukt. Bitte Gebrauchsanweisung beachten.

**EN (for reference):**
> Reliable blood-pressure measurement at home — clinically validated to [protocol/standard].
> Regular self-measurement helps you keep track of your readings between appointments. Ask your doctor how often you should measure.

What changed: the expert endorsement is gone entirely; the fear frame becomes a capability statement; the measurement-frequency instruction is handed back to the treating physician; and the validation claim is anchored to a protocol you can evidence (fill in the actual one — ESH-IP, ISO 81060-2, or whatever your file supports).

If you want the endorsement to survive somewhere, tell me and I'll draft a Fachkreise version with the gating and disclosure requirements spelled out.

# Device Claims Review: CGM marketing copy (3 lines, ~20 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Continuous glucose monitor, **Class IIa** (as stated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** **Publikum assumed** — "straight to your phone", second-person address, no gating. Confirm; if this is a trade-press or HCP-gated asset, HWG § 11 drops out (§ 3 does not).
**Markets:** EU assumed. **German market not confirmed** — HWG/UWG findings below are routed to `Also engaged` with that condition attached.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 0 OK.**

The intended purpose you supplied carries an express negative limitation — readings are *not* for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change — and all three lines run against it. "Dose with confidence" is the serious one: it is the payoff line, it names the exact use the assessed intended purpose excludes, and it is a limb (d) problem, which **evidence cannot cure**. No accuracy study fixes it; only narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment does.

**Ready to publish:** No, rewrite needed.

---

## Findings

### 1. "Dose with confidence."

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)** — and **Art. 7(b)** independently
**Why:** (d) prohibits "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". Insulin dosing is a treatment decision; the assessed intended purpose states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change". The copy suggests unqualified dosing off the device, which is the use the intended purpose carves out. (b) bites separately: an unconditional dosing instruction creates "a false impression regarding treatment" from a device whose assessed purpose is monitoring with an express treatment-decision limitation.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by narrowing the claim or by an intended purpose that covers non-adjunctive dosing.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (*"ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann"*) and § 11(1) no. 7 (health improved by use), **if the copy targets the German market and the audience is Publikum**. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit*, *von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse*), same condition.
**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** see rewrite below — replace with a line that positions the device as informing, not authorising, a dose.

### 2. "Real-time readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(a)** — ascribing a property the device does not have
**Why:** "Real-time" asserts that the reading reflects current blood glucose. The device measures **interstitial** glucose, and the lag between interstitial and blood glucose is the physiological reason your own intended purpose excludes rapid-change treatment decisions. A 5-minute *sampling interval* is not real-time equivalence to blood glucose; the copy conflates the two.
**Evidence needed:** the 5-minute measurement interval from the technical file (likely fine); nothing substantiates "real-time" against an interstitial measurand — that word goes regardless.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*wesentliche Merkmale ... Art, Ausführung, Risiken*), if DE market.
**Call:** **Needs rewording.**
**Suggested fix:** "A new interstitial glucose reading every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."

### 3. "Know your glucose at a glance."

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(b)** — false impression regarding the measurement
**Why:** "Your glucose", unqualified, reads as blood glucose to a patient audience. The distinction between interstitial and blood glucose is not pedantry here — it is the load-bearing element of the assessed intended purpose. "At a glance" compounds it by implying the number needs no interpretation or confirmation. This is the weakest of the three findings taken alone; it is a clear one in combination with lines 1 and 2, which is how the reader meets it.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by wording.
**Call:** **Needs rewording.**
**Suggested fix:** "See your glucose trend at a glance."

### 4. Omission across the asset — the rapid-change limitation

**Claim:** the asset as a whole (benefit-only, no limitation surfaced)
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(c)** — "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose"
**Why:** I am not inferring this risk from the device category — **you supplied it**. The intended purpose expressly records that readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. For a patient audience being told to dose, a reading relied on during rapid change is a likely risk in line with the intended purpose, and the copy surfaces nothing. Length is context and a 20-word ad cannot carry patient-facing safety text, so the proportionate fix is a short confirmatory-testing line, not a paragraph.
**Evidence needed:** the IFU wording for the rapid-change limitation, so the ad line matches it.
**Call:** **Needs rewording** (add the limitation).

---

## Paste-ready rewrite

> **Know your glucose trend at a glance.** A new interstitial glucose reading every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Confirm with a blood glucose test before treatment decisions when your glucose is changing quickly.

If "Dose with confidence" is commercially load-bearing and you want to keep that register, the honest version is about the *information*, not the dose:

> **Go into every dose informed.** A new interstitial glucose reading every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Confirm with a blood glucose test before treatment decisions when your glucose is changing quickly.

Both keep the headline rhythm and the 5-minute spec. Neither claims non-adjunctive dosing.

---

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Measurement interval as stated in the technical file / IFU | Regulatory affairs |
| Rapid-change limitation wording | IFU text, so the ad line tracks it rather than paraphrasing | Regulatory affairs |
| Audience | Is this asset gated to HCPs, or public? Determines whether HWG § 11 applies | Marketing |
| Market | Does this run in Germany? Determines whether HWG/UWG apply at all | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d)** — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a); § 11(1) no. 7** — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (conditional on DE market / Publikum)
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` (conditional on DE market)

I have not cited case law on how "real-time" or adjunctive-use claims have been treated in enforcement. That turns on BGH/OLG and notified-body practice this skill does not verify — if you have a source, point me at it and I will work from it rather than from memory.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`, and MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`, and MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — insulin dosing is a treatment decision. The assessed intended purpose states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change". Unqualified "dose with confidence" suggests a use "other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out".
- **(b)** — it creates "a false impression regarding treatment": that a reading alone is a sufficient basis to dose, in all conditions.
- **(c)** — the risk here is named in your own intended purpose, not inferred from the device category: readings may diverge from blood glucose during rapid change. Copy that instructs dosing while omitting the confirmation limitation fails to inform the patient "of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose". A dosing error in that window is the clinical consequence.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. A limb (d) breach is cured by narrowing the claim or by extending the conformity assessment to cover non-adjunctive (dosing) use. No accuracy study fixes the wording while the assessed purpose reads as it does.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" — if the copy runs in Germany, "with confidence" is a certainty-of-outcome framing attached to a dosing act, and § 3 no. 2(a) has no MDR Art. 7 equivalent. Also UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" — fitness and possible use), which is the UWG mirror of the same intended-purpose drift.
**Call:** **Cut.**
**Suggested fix:** See the paste-ready rewrite below. The line must be replaced by the confirmation instruction, not softened — "dose with more confidence" carries the same suggestion.

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** "Real-time" ascribes a property the device does not have. Your intended purpose implicitly concedes the point: the reason readings cannot replace BGM during rapid change is that interstitial glucose lags blood glucose. Copy calling the reading "real-time" tells the patient the number on the phone is the number in their blood right now, which is the specific misapprehension the intended purpose is written to prevent. "Every 5 minutes" is also in tension with "real-time" on the face of the sentence.
**Evidence needed:** The measurement/transmission interval from the technical documentation (confirm 5 minutes is the actual update cadence, not a best case), and how the IFU characterises physiological lag. Note that evidence cures the *interval* claim, not the word "real-time".
**Call:** **Needs rewording.**
**Suggested fix:** Drop "real-time"; state the cadence, which is the concrete and defensible claim. See rewrite.

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** none standing alone.
**Why:** Read in isolation this is a convenience claim about display, and "glucose" is conventional shorthand. It becomes a problem in context: it is the headline, and the asset-level limb (c) omission has to be cured somewhere. The headline is where a reader forms the impression that the phone number *is* their glucose value, full stop. Naming it as interstitial, or pairing it with trend, costs three words.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** **Needs rewording** — as part of curing the (c) omission across the asset, not as a standalone breach.
**Suggested fix:** See rewrite.

---

## Paste-ready rewrite

> **Know your glucose trend at a glance.** Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. **Confirm with a blood glucose test before dosing — always when your glucose is changing fast.** See the instructions for use.

What this preserves: the glanceability hook, the 5-minute cadence, the phone delivery. What it changes: "real-time" out (limb (a)); "dose with confidence" replaced by the confirmation instruction, which converts the limb (d) breach into a statement of the assessed purpose and simultaneously cures the limb (c) omission.

If marketing pushes back on losing the dosing line: the line is recoverable only by extending the conformity assessment to non-adjunctive use. That is a regulatory project, not a copy edit.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Actual measurement/transmission interval as stated in the technical documentation | RA / systems engineering |
| "real-time" | How the IFU characterises interstitial-to-blood lag; the rapid-change limitation wording | RA / clinical affairs |
| Whether any dosing claim is available at all | Whether the CE certificate covers non-adjunctive (dosing) use — your supplied intended purpose says no | RA / notified body file |
| Market and audience | Is this running in Germany? Is the page ungated and patient-facing? | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (conditional on German market)
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` (conditional on German market)

**Not engaged on this text:** HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12. There is no fear-of-not-using framing, no health-improvement-by-use claim, no advertorial format, no testimonial, and no under-14 targeting. I mention this because § 11 no. 7 is the high-frequency device finding and its absence here is worth stating rather than leaving implied. UWG § 6 is not engaged — the copy makes no comparison.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Two things would sharpen this if you have them: **is Germany a launch market** (it decides whether the § 3 no. 2(a) certainty finding is live or academic), and **the IFU's own wording on the rapid-change limitation** (the closer the fix tracks the IFU, the harder it is to attack).

## Device Claims Review: CGM marketing copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Class IIa CGM (continuous glucose monitor), MDR
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** Ambiguous — assumed **Publikum** (the copy speaks to the person wearing it: "your glucose", "your phone"). Confirm; if this is trade press, HWG § 11 drops out and § 3 still applies.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **Germany not confirmed** — HWG and UWG items below are therefore recorded as `Also engaged`, conditional on German-market targeting.

### Summary

5 items reviewed. **1 cut, 3 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.**

**Ready to publish: No, rewrite needed.**

The core problem is that the intended purpose contains an express carve-out — readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change — and the copy's closing line invites exactly the use the carve-out excludes. That is a limb (d) breach, and limb (d) is not cured by data.

---

### Findings

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d), and Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** Insulin dosing is a treatment decision. The assessed intended purpose states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change" — so the copy "suggest[s] uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out" (d), and creates "a false impression regarding treatment" (b) by presenting the reading as a sufficient basis to dose.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by narrowing the claim or by extending the conformity assessment to cover non-adjunctive dosing.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (*Erfolg mit Sicherheit* — "with confidence" as a promise of certain outcome) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit*), if the copy targets Germany `[verified]`
**Call:** **Cut**
**Suggested fix:** Replace with the confirmation instruction, not a dosing invitation — see revised copy below.

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) and (b) `[verified]`
**Why:** The device measures **interstitial** glucose. Unqualified "your glucose" ascribes a blood-glucose measurement property "which the device does not have" (a), and "know … at a glance" implies the reading alone is a complete and actionable picture, reinforcing the treatment-decision impression (b).
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the wording; the fix is the qualifier "interstitial".
**Call:** **Needs rewording**
**Suggested fix:** "Know your interstitial glucose at a glance."

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a), on "real-time" only `[verified]`
**Why:** The rapid-change carve-out in your own intended purpose is an acknowledgement that readings trail actual glucose when it moves quickly. "Real-time" asserts a simultaneity the assessed purpose implicitly denies. I am reading this off the supplied intended purpose, not inferring it from the device category.
**Evidence needed:** The 5-minute measurement interval, from the technical documentation — a spec claim, verifiable and cheap to defend once confirmed. Nothing substantiates "real-time".
**Call:** **Needs rewording**
**Suggested fix:** "Readings every 5 minutes" — drop "real-time".

---

**Claim:** *Asset-level omission* — the copy surfaces no limitation at all.
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:** (c) is an omission test: "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose." The risk is named in the material you supplied — reliance on CGM readings for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. This is benefit-only copy that actively invites that reliance and mentions no limitation or IFU. Given the asset invites dosing, an IFU pointer alone is not the proportionate fix here; the limitation belongs in the copy.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the IFU wording of the rapid-change limitation so the ad language tracks it.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(b) if any variant of this copy reassures about absence of harm; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*Risiken*), if Germany `[verified]`
**Call:** **Needs rewording** (add the limitation)
**Suggested fix:** See revised copy below.

---

**Claim:** "straight to your phone"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A factual delivery claim, not misleading on the material supplied.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the mobile app display is inside the CE certificate scope and the assessed intended purpose.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) and UWG § 5(2) no. 4 (*Zulassung … der Waren*), if smartphone display of readings is **not** within the assessed intended purpose / certificate scope `[verified]`
**Call:** **Verify**

---

### Revised copy (paste-ready)

> **Know your interstitial glucose at a glance.** Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. When your glucose is changing rapidly, confirm with a blood glucose test before making treatment decisions. Read the instructions for use.

This keeps the intent — continuous, convenient, on-phone — and drops only the dosing promise, which is the part that cannot be substantiated into compliance. If marketing wants a confidence line, "Confidence between fingersticks" stays inside the adjunctive framing; I'd still want that checked against the IFU wording before it ships.

### Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "every 5 minutes" | Measurement interval in the technical documentation | Regulatory / R&D |
| "straight to your phone" | Mobile app display within intended purpose and CE certificate scope | Regulatory (certificate + DoC) |
| Rapid-change limitation | Exact IFU wording, so ad copy tracks it | Regulatory (IFU) |
| Any "confidence" variant | Whether the device is assessed adjunctive-only or non-adjunctive | Notified body correspondence / DoC |

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a), § 3 no. 2(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 5(2) no. 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

2. **Audience** — if this is gated Fachkreise material, my Publikum assumption changes nothing in the findings above, since all of them run through Art. 7 and HWG § 3.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not approvable as written. One line ("Dose with confidence") sits outside the intended purpose in exactly the condition the intended purpose carves out, and the surrounding copy reinforces it. Two other lines need wording fixes. Rewrite below.

## Line by line

**"Know your glucose at a glance"**
- "your glucose" reads as blood glucose. The device measures *interstitial* glucose — a different analyte with a physiological lag. Use "sensor glucose" or "interstitial glucose" at least once in the headline block.
- "at a glance" is the softer half of the real problem: combined with the third line it tells users a look at the phone is sufficient. That's the behaviour the carve-out exists to prevent.

**"Real-time readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone"**
- "Real-time" overstates. Interstitial readings trail blood glucose, which is *why* rapid-change periods are excluded. "Continuous" or "updated every 5 minutes" is accurate and still compelling.
- "every 5 minutes" is a factual performance claim — fine if it matches the technical documentation exactly (measurement interval vs. display refresh vs. transmission interval are often three different numbers; cite the one the file supports).
- "straight to your phone" implies no preconditions. Needs a compatibility/connectivity qualifier somewhere on the asset, not necessarily in this line.

**"Dose with confidence"** — the blocker.
- Worth being precise about why: your intended purpose does *not* prohibit treatment decisions outright, only during rapid glucose change. So a dosing claim isn't inherently off-label here. What's off-label is an **unqualified** one. "Dose with confidence" asserts confidence uniformly, including in the one window where the device is documented as insufficient, and it does so while suppressing the confirmatory fingerstick.
- Under EU MDR Article 7 this is the textbook failure mode: a claim that misleads as to the device's intended purpose and performance, and omits information about a likely risk. Annex I Ch. III also requires promotional claims to be consistent with the IFU; "dose with confidence" cannot be reconciled with a rapid-change confirmation requirement.
- Reviewer-facing risk: this single line is enough to make a notified body or competent authority question whether your marketing reflects a broader non-adjunctive intended purpose than the one you certified.

## Suggested rewrite

Option A — keeps the dosing benefit, qualified:

> **Your glucose, continuously.**
> Sensor glucose readings updated every 5 minutes, straight to your phone.
> Dose with confidence — and confirm with a fingerstick when your glucose is changing fast.

Option B — drops the dosing claim, leans on trend awareness (lowest regulatory friction):

> **See where your glucose is heading.**
> Continuous sensor glucose, updated every 5 minutes, on your phone.
> Spot the trends between fingersticks.

Either way, the asset needs a visible qualifier, not buried in 6pt legal:

> For adults with diabetes. Sensor readings measure interstitial glucose and are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change. Requires a compatible smartphone.

I'd go with Option A. It preserves the commercially valuable claim, and the qualifier arguably *builds* trust rather than undercutting it — it reads as the product knowing its own limits.

## Two things to confirm before sign-off

1. **Which interval is substantiated** — pull the exact figure from the technical documentation for the 5-minute claim.
2. **Market scope.** The above is EU MDR reasoning. If this runs in the US, the analysis differs materially: FDA distinguishes adjunctive from integrated CGM (iCGM special controls), and a dosing claim maps to a specific cleared indication rather than to an intended-purpose carve-out. If the US indication is adjunctive, Option A's dosing line is not usable there at all and you'd need Option B for that market. Worth a two-line check with RA rather than assuming the EU wording travels.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not approvable as written. One line ("Dose with confidence") contradicts a stated limitation in the intended purpose, and two others drift from the labelled claim. Under MDR Art. 7, promotional material can't mislead about intended purpose, performance, or function — and claims have to be traceable to the clinical evaluation and IFU.

---

### "Know your glucose at a glance"

**Minor — recommend change.** The device measures *interstitial* glucose. The entire reason for the rapid-change caveat is that interstitial and blood glucose diverge, so a headline that conflates them undermines the limitation you're obliged to communicate. "Know your glucose" is common category language and is probably defensible, but it's a cheap fix to make it accurate.

"At a glance" is fine.

### "Real-time readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone"

**Check against technical documentation.** Two things to verify rather than assume:

- **"Real-time"** is a recognised category term (rtCGM as distinct from intermittently-scanned/flash), so it's likely defensible *as a category descriptor*. But paired with "every 5 minutes" in the same sentence it reads as a latency claim, and every CGM has physiological interstitial lag plus algorithm delay. If your IFU quantifies lag, the copy shouldn't imply zero.
- **"Every 5 minutes"** and **"straight to your phone"** are factual performance claims — confirm both match the IFU exactly (sampling vs. display interval; whether phone delivery requires the reader/app, a supported-device list, or Bluetooth proximity).

### "Dose with confidence"

**Blocker.** Your intended purpose permits dosing *except* during rapid glucose change — so this isn't off-label in the absolute, but it's unqualified in a way that erases the one carve-out you're required to state. It's also the highest-risk possible framing of that carve-out: it tells a user to feel most confident in exactly the situation (a fast rise or fall) where the label says to confirm with a fingerstick.

Compounding this: nothing in the copy carries the limitation, the population (adults with diabetes), or a direction to the IFU.

---

## Suggested rewrite

> **Know your glucose at a glance.**
> Real-time interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone.
> Confirm with a fingerstick when your glucose is changing quickly.
>
> *For adults with diabetes. Readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change. Read the Instructions for Use.*

This keeps the rhythm of the original and keeps a dosing-adjacent promise, but moves the confidence from the act of dosing to the act of knowing.

If marketing wants to retain a dosing benefit explicitly, the qualified version is: *"Dose without routine fingersticks — confirm when glucose is changing fast."* That's claimable on your stated intended purpose and still differentiates.

## Open questions for you

1. **Medium and placement.** Whether the limitation statement can sit as a footnote or must be in the primary field of vision depends on format (banner ad vs. packaging vs. HCP detail aid) and market. A 300×250 banner may not accommodate it — in which case the dosing claim should come out entirely and live on the landing page instead.
2. **Markets.** The above is MDR-framed. If this runs in the US, FDA's iCGM classification and the specific cleared indication drive different wording, and non-adjunctive dosing claims need the labelling to support them.
3. **Substantiation file.** "Every 5 minutes" and any accuracy implication need a pointer to the clinical evaluation report section that supports them.

This is a copy review, not regulatory sign-off — your RA function should hold the final claim-to-label traceability check before release.
