graders.evidence:
## Verdict

**Do not ship as written.** One blocking issue, two that need fixing, plus missing mandatory elements.

I'm assuming EU MDR 2017/745 (and/or UK MDR 2002) given "Class IIa" — flag if this is for another market, as the analysis changes.

---

### 🔴 Blocking: "Dose with confidence"

This is an unqualified insulin-dosing claim. Your intended purpose explicitly says readings are **not** intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change — so the device is adjunctive in exactly the situation where dosing errors hurt most.

- **MDR Article 7** prohibits claims that mislead regarding intended purpose, or that "ascribe functions to the device which the device does not have."
- Practically: this is off-label promotion of a non-adjunctive use the device isn't cleared for. It's also the claim a regulator or plaintiff's counsel reaches for first after a hypoglycaemia event, because it directly contradicts the IFU.
- "With confidence" makes it worse — it's a reassurance claim layered on a use the label warns against.

No qualifier or asterisk rescues this. Cut the dosing claim.

### 🟠 "Real-time readings every 5 minutes"

Two separate problems:

1. **"Real-time"** — interstitial glucose lags blood glucose (typically ~5–10 min, longest during rapid change). "Real-time" implies the opposite and undercuts the very limitation your intended purpose is built around. Note it's an accepted term of art in the field ("rtCGM"), but in consumer-facing headline copy next to a dosing claim it reads as a performance representation, not a category label.
2. **"Every 5 minutes"** — a specific performance claim. Must match the sampling/display interval in the technical documentation and IFU exactly. Verify before approval; if the sensor samples at one rate and displays at another, say the displayed rate.

### 🟠 "Know your glucose at a glance"

- Measurand is **interstitial** glucose, not blood glucose. Your own intended purpose draws that distinction; the copy erases it.
- No indicated population. Intended purpose is *adults with diabetes*; unqualified "know your glucose" invites wellness/non-diabetic and paediatric readings — both off-label.

### 🟡 Missing mandatory / expected elements

- Identification as a medical device (some member states require explicit wording, e.g. DE "Medizinprodukt" per HWG).
- "Read the instructions for use" / consult-the-IFU statement.
- The fingerstick-confirmation limitation, stated affirmatively rather than buried.
- Prescription status and CE mark / UKCA presentation per your regulatory strategy.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**Option A — keeps the energy, drops the risk:**

> **Your glucose trend, at a glance.**
> Sensor glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. See where you're heading, not just where you are.

**Option B — more conservative:**

> **See your glucose trends on your phone.**
> Continuous interstitial glucose readings, updated every 5 minutes, for adults with diabetes.

**Required adjacent text (not a footnote in 6pt):**

> Interstitial glucose readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement. Confirm with a fingerstick before treatment decisions, particularly when your glucose is changing rapidly. For adults with diabetes. [Medical device. Read the instructions for use.]

---

## The trade you're actually making

The headline value of a CGM *is* trend and direction — that's the thing a fingerstick can't give you, and it's fully on-label. Option A leans into that, so you lose very little persuasive force by dropping "Dose with confidence."

Two things to route onward:
- **Confirm the 5-minute interval** against the technical file / IFU before sign-off.
- **Get regulatory/legal sign-off on final wording** — I'm flagging risk, not clearing copy, and member-state advertising rules vary (Germany's HWG and France's ANSM pre-vetting regime are the usual pinch points).

# Device Claims Review: comparison block (3-sentence copy)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** unnamed Class I software device (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise as stated (manufacturers, regulatory consultants) — HWG § 11 not applied
**Markets:** DE (EU rules apply throughout)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 2 reword, 0 substantiate, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No, rewrite needed.

The dominant problem is structural, not evidentiary: the copy compares against an unnamed comparator with a quantified figure. No amount of internal data fixes that.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Half the rework of what most teams use today."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]`; UWG § 6(2) no. 1 `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 6(2) no. 2 requires the comparison to rest on **nachprüfbare** characteristics — the *reader* must be able to check it. "What most teams use today" names no product, and "half the rework" defines no metric, baseline, sample or period, so nothing here is checkable from public information. § 6(2) no. 1 fails ahead of that: with the comparator undefined, you cannot show it serves the **gleichen Bedarf oder dieselbe Zweckbestimmung** — relevant for a Class I device, where the counterpart tooling may not be a device at all. Independently, "Half the rework" is an Angabe over **von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse** under § 5(2) no. 1, and "most teams" asserts market prevalence as fact.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for § 6(2) no. 2 — cannot be cured by evidence. Verifiability is about what the reader can check, so a sound internal study does not rescue an undefined comparator. Curable only by naming the comparator and publishing the basis, or dropping the comparison. If you keep it, you then also need the study (metric definition, n, period, method) to satisfy § 5(2) no. 1.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(1) is the gate — if the market cannot identify any competitor from "what most teams use today", § 6 does not engage and this falls to § 5(2) no. 1 alone. In a comparison block on a vendor page, sitting next to the "spreadsheet-and-email" line, identification is the likelier reading. The fix is the same either way.
**Call:** Cut (or rebuild as a named, sourced comparison)

---

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits **ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have**. "Them" refers back to "their errors" without restriction, so the sentence claims the device catches the reader's submission errors — all of them — with no stated condition, scope or error class. Unless the performance data supports detection of every error type in scope, this is capability stated without its qualifying condition. Same defect under § 5(2) no. 1 as **Zwecktauglichkeit** and **von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse**.
**Evidence needed:** the detection scope and performance data — which error classes are checked, against which rule set or standard, with what sensitivity. This limb *is* curable by evidence plus a scoped restatement.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — **ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann** — an unconditional "we catch them" is a certainty-of-outcome shape. Caveat I want to be straight about: § 3 no. 2(a) speaks of "Erfolg" and the surrounding provision is framed around therapeutic effect, while your "Erfolg" is a workflow outcome. Whether no. 2(a) reaches a non-clinical outcome claim is a question of interpretation, and the case law that would settle it is outside what this review verifies. Treat it as live risk to raise with counsel, not as a call I can source.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** Asserted as fact about the results others obtain ("still find their errors after submission"), stated absolutely and about an entire cohort. It is an Angabe about **von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse** and, via § 5(1), capable of moving a purchasing decision in your favour on an unsupported factual premise.
**Evidence needed:** n/a as phrased — an absolute statement about all spreadsheet-and-email users is not substantiable. Reframe as a description of a failure mode rather than an assertion about a group.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 5 `[verified]` (**herabsetzt oder verunglimpft**) — "the crowd" is dismissive of the people, not the method — but only if § 6(1) **Erkennbarkeit** is satisfied, i.e. if the market reads "spreadsheet-and-email" as identifying particular competitors' products rather than generic manual practice. If it reads as generic practice, § 6 does not engage and only § 5 applies. I am not going to predict which reading prevails; the rewrite below removes the question.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

### Paste-ready rewrite

Two versions, depending on whether you can publish comparison data.

**Option A — comparison dropped (publishable without new evidence):**

> Errors in a submission dossier are often found only after filing, when correction is slowest. [Product] runs completeness and consistency checks against [rule set / standard] before you file, and flags [error classes covered]. See [link] for the checks covered and their limits.

**Option B — comparison kept (requires a published basis):**

> In a [period] comparison against [named comparator], teams using [Product] recorded [X]% less post-submission rework across [n] submissions. Method and full results: [link].

Option B satisfies § 6(2) no. 2 only if the comparator is named, the metric is defined, and the link is live at publication. "Leading tools" or "manual processes" in the comparator slot puts you back where you started.

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I cannot tell from what you have supplied whether the IFU records a **likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose** that belongs here — for instance, whether users must not treat a clean check result as confirmation that a dossier is complete. I will not infer a risk from the device category and flag the omission on that basis. Worth checking against the IFU; if such a limitation exists, a short pointer to it is usually the proportionate fix for copy this short.

### Limb (d) — not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Specifically, "we catch them before [submission]" positions the product as a submission-quality gate; if the assessed intended purpose is narrower than that, the sentence is a (d) problem as well as the (a) problem above — and (d) is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment, not by data. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "We catch them before" | Detection scope: error classes checked, rule set/standard, performance data | Product / QA |
| "Half the rework…" (if kept) | Named comparator, metric definition, n, period, method — publishable | Marketing + counsel |
| Limb (c) check | Whether the IFU records a likely risk or limitation for marketing to surface | RA / technical file owner |
| Limb (d) check | Intended purpose verbatim from DoC / technical documentation | RA |

- **HWG § 11** — you state the audience is Fachkreise, so § 11 does not apply. For what it is worth, nothing in this copy hits nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 or 12 even on a Publikum reading: there is no health-impairment-by-non-use framing, no testimonial, no unlabelled advertorial. If the block sits on an ungated public page, that changes the § 11 analysis in principle but not the outcome here.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** — the copy makes no claim about class, CE scope, notified-body involvement or certification, so there is nothing to flag. Worth keeping in mind as you rewrite: for a Class I device, adding anything that implies notified-body involvement would be a § 5(2) no. 4 finding on its own.

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (applicability to non-clinical outcome claims flagged as interpretive)
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7–9, 11, 12 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (not applicable; audience is Fachkreise)
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 1, 2, 5 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

Enforcement here arrives as an Abmahnung from a competitor with a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung and costs attached — no regulator needs to act — and an undefined comparator is the cheapest possible target because the defect is visible on the face of the copy. ## Verdict

Two claims in this block are legally exposed in Germany, and the framing works against the audience you named. I'd not ship it as written.

---

### 1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — highest risk

This is a quantified comparative superiority claim against an unnamed but identifiable class of competitors.

- **UWG §6(2)**: comparative advertising is only lawful where it compares objectively, on verifiable, relevant, representative features. "What most teams use today" isn't a defined comparison basis — you can't verify a claim against an undefined baseline, and courts read that as failure of the verifiability condition rather than as harmless vagueness.
- **UWG §5**: independently attackable as misleading. In Germany the burden of substantiation sits with you, and for a device performance claim it's a high bar — you need the study, sample, definition of "rework," and measurement method ready *before* publication, not after an Abmahnung.
- **Practical exposure**: competitors and the Wettbewerbszentrale can issue a cease-and-desist with cost-shifting. This is cheap for them and expensive for you.

Fix: convert it to a self-referential, disclosed-method claim ("teams reduced rework cycles by X% vs. their own prior process, n=…, method linked"), or drop the number.

### 2. "We catch them before" — MDR Article 7 and intended-purpose scope

"Catch" reads as an absolute: *all* errors, reliably. If the tool flags defined categories of issues, the copy overstates performance, which is exactly what Art. 7 prohibits — claims that mislead as to performance.

Second, and worth resolving before anything else: **does "catching submission errors" appear in the intended purpose in your technical documentation?** If not, this is promotion outside the declared intended purpose. There's also a mismatch I can't resolve from the copy alone — a regulatory-submission tool for manufacturers is not usually itself a Class I device, and Class I general (non-Is/Im/Ir) involves self-certification, not a notified-body "submission." Either the block is describing a product other than the regulated device, or "submission" needs to be precise about what is filed and to whom. Please confirm which.

HWG §3 also applies (misleading advertising for Medizinprodukte), though since your audience is Fachkreise, the §11 public-advertising restrictions don't bite.

### 3. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — audience and tone

Your stated audience *is* the spreadsheet-and-email crowd. You're mocking the buyer's current workflow and, by extension, the RA consultant who set it up. Beyond the conversion problem, this invites a disparagement argument (UWG §4 Nr. 1) since the class is identifiable in a small vendor market.

It also localizes badly. "Crowd" has no neutral German equivalent here — "die Excel-und-E-Mail-Fraktion" lands as open contempt, and this audience rewards Sachlichkeit.

---

### Suggested rewrite

> "Documentation errors usually surface after filing. [Product] checks [defined artifact] against [defined ruleset] while you work, so gaps appear while they're still cheap to fix. In [study, n=…], teams cut rework cycles by [X]% against their previous process — [method]."

Keeps the before/after contrast that makes the original work, drops the competitor comparison and the insult, and puts a verifiable number where an unverifiable one was.

**Before this goes live, I need from you:** the intended-purpose wording from the technical documentation, and whatever evidence backs the "half the rework" figure. If the evidence is a customer anecdote rather than a study, say so and I'll write a version that doesn't quantify.

**1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — highest risk**

An unverifiable quantified comparison. Under § 6 UWG a comparison must rest on objective, verifiable characteristics; "what most teams use today" names no comparator and defines no metric, so nobody can check it. That makes it misleading under § 5 UWG regardless of whether a competitor is identifiable. In German practice the burden of proof for a superiority claim sits with the advertiser, and a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale can bring an Abmahnung cheaply, with an Unterlassungserklärung and contractual penalty attached.

To keep the number you need, on file and referenced in the copy: comparator, metric (rework hours? review cycles? findings per submission?), sample size, study date, and methodology — available to the reader on request.

Separately, "what most teams use today" is itself a factual market-share assertion that needs evidence.

**2. "We catch them before" — absolute performance claim**

"Catch" reads as guaranteed detection. If this is the Class I device, MDR Art. 7 prohibits claims that ascribe functions the device doesn't have or mislead as to performance, and the claim must be consistent with the intended purpose in your technical documentation. Soften to detection *support*: flags, surfaces, helps identify. Also avoid any drift toward implying regulatory acceptance — catching errors is not the same as a successful submission.

**3. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — commercial, not legal**

This insults the exact people you're selling to. Regulatory consultants and QM leads *are* the spreadsheet-and-email crowd, largely by choice and validation burden. In German the register lands worse: "die Excel-und-E-Mail-Fraktion" is flippant where this audience expects Sachlichkeit. It also risks being read as Herabsetzung of competitors whose products are spreadsheet-based (§ 6 Abs. 2 Nr. 5 UWG), though that's the weaker of the two problems.

**4. Copy is in English for a German market**

The idioms here ("crowd", the clipped "We catch them before") don't survive translation. Write the German first rather than translating this.

## Rewrites

**If you have the data** (substantiate the number, drop the jab):

> Dokumentationsfehler zeigen sich oft erst nach der Einreichung. [Produkt] prüft Ihre Unterlagen vorher und weist auf Lücken hin — in einer Erhebung unter [N] Anwendern (Stand: [Datum]) reduzierte sich der Nachbearbeitungsaufwand um [X] % gegenüber [konkreter Vergleichsprozess].¹
>
> ¹ Methodik und Datengrundlage auf Anfrage.

**If you don't** (no number, no comparison):

> Lücken finden, bevor Sie einreichen — nicht danach. Strukturierte Prüfungen statt Abstimmung per Excel und E-Mail.

The second version keeps the spreadsheet contrast as a description of a *workflow* rather than a swipe at the people using it, and makes no comparative or quantified claim at all. That's the version I'd ship while the substantiation file gets built.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't ship as written. Two claims carry real UWG/MDR exposure, and the framing insults the people you're selling to.

## Issues, by severity

**1. "Half the rework" — unsubstantiated quantitative comparative claim (high)**
A specific numeric superiority claim against an unnamed comparator group. Under UWG §5 and §6 the burden of proof sits with you, and it must be discharged *at time of publication* — you cannot commission the study after a competitor's `Abmahnung` lands. You need a defined baseline ("rework" = what, measured how?), a named or clearly delimited comparator, a representative sample, and a documented methodology. Note also that HWG §3 applies (medical devices fall under HWG §1(1) No. 1a), and if you cite a study to support the number, HWG §6 requires it be identifiable and accurately represented.

**2. "We catch them before" — absolute detection claim (high)**
Reads as exhaustive error detection. If the software cannot guarantee catching all errors — and it can't — this ascribes performance the device does not have: MDR Art. 7 (misleading as to performance) plus UWG §5. Needs a scope qualifier naming what class of errors is checked.

**3. Implied intended purpose vs. CE-marked intended purpose (high — needs an answer)**
The copy positions the product as submission QA for manufacturers. Is that the registered intended purpose in your technical documentation? If the CE-marked purpose is narrower, this is promotion outside intended purpose and Art. 7 bites on the *positioning*, not just the wording. Also worth confirming separately: Class I for standalone software is unusual under MDR Rule 11, and regulatory consultants in this audience will notice and ask. Make sure the classification rationale is defensible before you put the claim in front of them.

**4. "Most teams use today" — implicit market-share claim (medium)**
"Most" is a factual assertion about prevalence, independently actionable under UWG §5. Either evidence it or drop the quantifier ("many teams").

**5. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — audience mismatch (medium, commercial not legal)**
Your buyers *are* the spreadsheet-and-email crowd. The line asks them to accept an insult before they accept your argument. Disparagement under UWG §6(2)(5) is aimed at competitors, so the legal risk here is thin — but this is a conservative `Fachkreise` audience that expects a `sachlich` register, and the phrase has no clean German rendering. Localized, "crowd" lands as condescension.

**6. "Still find their errors after submission" (medium)**
A negative factual claim about outcomes for users of competing methods. Same substantiation burden as #1.

**7. Broken comparison (low)**
"Half the rework of what most teams use today" compares rework to a *tool*. Category mismatch — should be "of the tools most teams use."

## Rewrites

**Conservative (no substantiation file needed):**
> "Submission errors are expensive to find late. Our pre-submission checks surface [format, completeness, and traceability] gaps before you file."

**Substantiated (if you have the data):**
> "In [study, 2026, n=NN], teams using [Product] reported NN% less post-submission rework than teams working from spreadsheets and email. Pre-submission checks cover [defined scope]."

Note the neutral framing of the comparator — "working from spreadsheets and email" describes a method, not a class of person. Method comparison (`Systemvergleich`) is permissible under German law and costs you nothing rhetorically.

## Before sign-off

- Substantiation file for any retained number, dated before publication
- Definition of "rework" that a third party could reproduce
- Confirmation that the marketed function sits inside the CE-marked intended purpose
- Defined scope of what the checks do and do not detect
- German copy reviewed for register, not just translated — the idiom won't survive

Happy to draft the German version once you've settled which claims survive substantiation.

# Device Claims Review: "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Wound dressing, Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED** — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** **Ambiguous** — see note below
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

1 claim reviewed. 1 rewrite needed.

**Ready to publish:** No, rewrite needed.

The important finding is that "40% faster" has **no comparator**. Faster than what? Standard gauze? A named competitor? No dressing? Untreated? That defect sits on the face of the copy and no amount of clinical data fixes it. Your n=12 study is a real problem too, but it's the second problem, and fixing the study wouldn't fix the first one.

## Finding

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`; HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`

**Why:**
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** reaches "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" *and* "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**". A bare "40%" presents a test result while withholding every essential component of that test: the comparator, the arm structure, n, the endpoint, who ran it. The figure is presented as a product property when it is a single unpublished in-house result.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** — "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". The copy is unconditional indicative: the dressing *heals* 40% faster, full stop, no range, no patient population, no "in einer Studie". Stated that way it reads as a promised outcome rather than an observed one. The unhedged phrasing is what triggers this limb, which is why the fix is partly grammatical.
- **MDR Art. 7(a)** — ascribing a property the device does not have. A 40% acceleration in healing is a performance property, and the whole evidentiary basis is one unpublished single-site study with 12 subjects.

**Evidence needed:** For the § 5 and Art. 7(a) limbs — a named comparator, a controlled comparative design, and the test's essential components disclosed at the point of claim. **What study quality suffices is the case-law question I declined**; the statute doesn't set a threshold. For § 3 no. 2(a): n/a, cured by rewording, not data.

**Also engaged:**
- **MDR Art. 7(d)**, if the assessed intended purpose for this dressing is framed as protecting the wound / maintaining a moist wound environment rather than *accelerating healing*. Class IIa dressings very often are. If so, "heals 40% faster" asserts an effect outside the conformity assessment, and that **cannot be cured by evidence** — only by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment. Check this first; it may make the substantiation question moot.
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2**, if anything in the surrounding copy makes a competitor recognisable ("unlike conventional dressings", a category the market reads as a specific brand). § 6(1)'s "erkennbar" is broad. If it bites, the claim fails on *nachprüfbar* — verifiability is about what the **reader** can check, so your internal study, however sound, cannot rescue it.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7**, if the audience is Publikum — "Gesundheit [...] durch die Verwendung verbessert". For devices only nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 apply. I've left this conditional rather than asserting it, because an efficacy claim squarely inside an assessed healing-related intended purpose sits differently under no. 7 than "don't leave your health to chance" does.

**Call:** Needs rewording **and** substantiation.

**Suggested fix** — paste-ready, both directions:

*Option A, drop the figure (works for Publikum):*
> „[Produktname] — feuchte Wundversorgung für [Indikation aus der Zweckbestimmung]. Schützt die Wunde und unterstützt ein feuchtes Wundmilieu."

Lift the bracketed text verbatim from the Zweckbestimmung in your DoC. That keeps you inside Art. 7(d) by construction.

*Option B, keep the figure, Fachkreise material only, with full disclosure:*
> „In einer monozentrischen, nicht publizierten Anwendungsbeobachtung des Herstellers (n = 12, einarmig, [Jahr]) war die mittlere Zeit bis zum Wundverschluss gegenüber [genau benannter Komparator] um 40 % kürzer. Einzelstudie ohne Kontrollgruppe und ohne Verblindung; Ergebnis nicht extern validiert."

Option B discloses the essential components § 5(2) no. 1 asks about and drops the certainty framing § 3 no. 2(a) catches. Whether it *survives* is the case-law question — an n=12 uncontrolled in-house study carrying a quantified superiority figure is exactly the fact pattern I'd expect a competitor to test by Abmahnung, and I can't tell you how that lands.

**Open question on limb (c):** the copy surfaces no limitation or contraindication. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs in the copy. Worth checking against the IFU — I won't invent one from the device category.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Item | Needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Zweckbestimmung as assessed | Verbatim from DoC / technical documentation | RA/QA |
| Whether "accelerated healing" is inside it | Yes/no — gates everything above | RA/QA |
| Comparator for "40%" | Named product or named standard of care | Clinical |
| Study essentials | Design, arms, endpoint, site, n, publication status | Clinical |
| Audience for the asset | Gated Fachkreise vs. open web | Marketing |
| Any recognisable competitor in surrounding copy | Full asset, not just the headline | Marketing |

## To ask counsel

1. What substantiation standard do the German courts apply to a quantified efficacy claim for a Class IIa device — and specifically, is an uncontrolled unpublished in-house study with n=12 capable of supporting a "40% faster" claim at all, or is it disqualified by design regardless of disclosure?
2. Who bears the burden if we're abgemahnt — must we prove the figure, or must they disprove it?
3. Does the disclosure in Option B cure enough, or does the number have to come out of consumer-facing copy entirely?

Bring them the Zweckbestimmung and the study protocol; those two documents will drive their answer more than the copy will.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), 7(c), 7(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a), § 11(1) no. 7 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Paste the Zweckbestimmung and I'll assess limb (d) — given a Class IIa dressing, that's the limb most likely to decide this, and it's the one where data won't help you.

# Device Claims Review: "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Class IIa wound dressing
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Not stated — § 11 finding flagged conditionally below
**Markets:** DE (HWG + UWG overlay applies), EU

## Summary

1 claim reviewed. 1 cut.

**Ready to publish:** No, rewrite needed.

The important finding is that this claim's main problem isn't the size of your study. Two of the breaches below cannot be cured by evidence at all — not by n=12, not by n=1200.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."
**Breach:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 3 no. 2(a) prohibits copy falsely creating the impression "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". This is a flat indicative — no "up to", no "can", no population qualifier. It states a 40% acceleration as what the dressing does, not as an average observed under study conditions. § 5(2) no. 1 reaches "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**": the figure is presented as an established property of the device with no disclosure that it derives from a single unpublished in-house study, and the omission of that basis is itself capable of deceiving ("zur Täuschung geeignet").
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]` — "40% faster" is a comparison with no stated comparator. Faster than no dressing? Than standard gauze? Than a named competitor? If the German market can tell who or what is meant, § 6(1) is engaged ("erkennbar" is broad, the competitor need not be named), and the comparison then fails no. 2's **nachprüfbar** limb on the face of the copy. Note this is structural: verifiability is about what *the reader* can check from public information, so an unpublished study cannot cure it however sound it is.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and (b) `[verified]` — ascribing a quantified healing-acceleration property, and the treatment impression that goes with it, if the performance data in the technical file does not carry the figure.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — **the one to check first.** If the assessed intended purpose is framed as exudate management, wound protection, maintaining a moist wound environment (typical for Class IIa dressings) rather than *accelerating healing*, then an accelerated-healing claim suggests a use outside what the conformity assessment covered. That breach is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment — **not by data.** Paste the intended purpose from the DoC and I'll assess this properly.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` — health "durch die Verwendung verbessert" framing, if the audience is Publikum. An ungated public product page counts; a page being technical doesn't make it Fachkreise. Tell me which and I'll call it.
**Evidence needed:** For § 5(2) no. 1, a substantiated and disclosed basis for the figure. For § 3 no. 2(a) and § 6(2) no. 2, **n/a — cannot be cured by evidence.**
**Call:** Cut.
**Suggested fix (paste-ready):**

> Designed to support wound healing in a moist wound environment.

If you want to keep the study in play, the figure has to move out of the headline claim and into disclosed, verifiable data — which means publishing it:

> In a single-centre in-house study (n=12), wounds treated with [Device] closed on average 40% faster than with [named comparator]. Preliminary data from a small study; not confirmed in a controlled trial. [Citation / link to published study.]

Without publication, the bracketed citation is the part you can't fill, and § 6(2) no. 2 stays breached if the comparison identifies a competitor. My recommendation: run with the first version now, and revisit the figure if and when the study is published and powered.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Item | Needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Intended purpose as assessed | Verbatim from DoC / technical documentation | RA/QA |
| Does the technical file's clinical evaluation support any healing-rate claim? | Yes/no + wording | RA/QA |
| Comparator for "40% faster" | Named product or defined standard of care | Clinical/marketing |
| Publication status and route for the n=12 study | Timeline | Clinical |
| Audience for this asset | Fachkreise or Publikum | Marketing |
| Likely risk in the IFU | Does the IFU record one that benefit-only copy should surface? | RA/QA |

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here under Art. 7(c), so I haven't raised it — worth checking against the IFU.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) no. 7 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- BGH substantiation standard for device efficacy claims — `[verify]`, not assessed, see top

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Wound dressing, Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Ambiguous — assessed for both; see note below
**Markets:** DE (EU layer applies throughout)

## Summary

1 claim reviewed. 1 needs rewording **and** substantiation.

**Ready to publish:** No, rewrite needed.

The headline issue is not that n=12 is thin — though it is. It's that the claim has **no comparator**. "40% faster" than what? No dressing? Standard gauze? A named competitor? Wet-to-dry? A reader cannot check the figure against anything, and that defect sits on the face of the copy. More evidence does not cure it; only naming the baseline does.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Breach:**
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** [verified] — on two of the listed circumstances: "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**". The copy publishes a quantified test result while withholding the essential components of the test — that it is a single in-house study, n=12, unpublished, and what it compared against. A bare percentage with no baseline is zur Täuschung geeignet independently of whether 40% is the correct number.
- **MDR Art. 7(a)** [verified] — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". The claim is unrestricted as to wound type, aetiology and patient population; it says "wounds", full stop. An n=12 study cannot have covered that scope. The breach is the gap between the width of the claim and the width of the evidence, not the 40% itself.
- **HWG § 3 no. 1** [verified] — same test in the German layer: "eine therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen beigelegt werden, die sie nicht haben". Cite alongside Art. 7(a) for the German market; per the mapping table these are essentially the same test, and the German one is what an Abmahnung will run on.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** [verified] — "fälschlich der Eindruck erweckt wird, daß ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". Unconditional present indicative, no qualifier, no range, no "kann". As four words standing alone it reads as the result every user gets. This limb has **no MDR Art. 7 equivalent**, so it is invisible to an EU-only review. Push back if the surrounding asset carries qualifying language — I'm assessing the copy as given.

**Evidence needed:** For Art. 7(a) / § 3 no. 1 — a study whose population and wound type match the width of the claim as written, or a claim narrowed to match the study you have. For § 5(2) no. 1 — nothing; disclosure of the test's essential components is a drafting fix, not an evidence gap.

**Also engaged:**
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2** [verified] — "nicht objektiv auf eine oder mehrere wesentliche, relevante, **nachprüfbare** und typische Eigenschaften ... bezogen", *if* the full asset makes a competitor or competing product recognisable under § 6(1). "Erkennbar" is broad and does not require naming anyone — if the surrounding page positions this against conventional dressings such that the market can tell who is meant, you are in comparative advertising and the undefined comparator breaches no. 2 on its face. Worth flagging clearly: **your n=12 study, however sound, cannot fix this one.** Nachprüfbarkeit is about what the *reader* can verify from public information, not what you hold in the technical file. An unpublished study is by definition not nachprüfbar.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** [verified] — "Werbeaussagen, die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit ... durch die Verwendung verbessert werden könnte", *if* the audience is Publikum. Weaker ground here than usual, since a wound dressing's whole assessed purpose is wound healing and stating your intended purpose can't itself be a no. 7 breach. But a quantified superiority-of-outcome framing goes beyond stating the purpose. Depends on the audience call below.

**Call:** Needs rewording **and** substantiation.

**Suggested fix** — two options, paste-ready:

**A. Drop the figure (recommended).**
> Wundauflage zur Unterstützung der Wundheilung.

This tracks the intended purpose, carries no comparator, and needs no study. It is dull and it is cheap to defend.

**B. Keep the figure, fully qualified.** Only if the assessed intended purpose covers accelerated healing (see below) and you accept the residual risk:
> In einer einarmigen Anwendungsbeobachtung des Herstellers (n=12, [Wundtyp]) schloss sich die Wunde im Mittel 40 % schneller als unter [konkrete Vergleichsbehandlung]. Nicht publizierte Einzelstudie; die Ergebnisse sind nicht auf andere Wundarten übertragbar.

Candidly: option B discloses the weakness so plainly that it stops working as marketing, which is the honest signal that the figure isn't ready to headline. I'd hold the 40% for a published, controlled study and ship A now.

## Not assessed

**Limb (d) — uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is not assessed: I have not seen the intended purpose.** Paste it from the technical documentation or the DoC and I'll cover it.

Flagging it hard, because on these facts it is the most dangerous limb and the one people don't see coming. If the intended purpose your notified body assessed is framed as, say, "absorption of exudate and protection of the wound", then a *faster healing* performance claim suggests a use outside what the conformity assessment covered — and a limb (d) breach is **not curable by evidence**. A better study would not help. It is cured only by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment. So check that before you spend money on a bigger trial.

**Limb (c) — failing to inform of a likely risk:** the copy surfaces no limitation, but I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs in the copy. I won't infer one from "wound dressing" — that would be an unfalsifiable finding. Worth checking against the IFU.

**Audience:** you haven't told me, and I'm not going to default to Fachkreise because the product is technical — that's the assumption that under-flags. If this runs anywhere ungated and consumer-facing (pharmacy shelf, product page, Apotheken-Umschau), § 11 applies and no. 7 is live. If it's trade press or hospital procurement only, § 11 drops out entirely and § 3 still applies. Confirm which.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "40% faster" | Intended purpose verbatim from the DoC / technical file — gates limb (d) | RA/QA |
| "40% faster" | The comparator actually used in the n=12 study, stated concretely | Clinical / study author |
| "40% faster" | Wound type and population in the study, to size the claim | Clinical |
| "40% faster" | Whether IFU records a likely risk that the copy must surface | RA/QA |
| — | Publication status and route, if the figure is to survive long-term | Clinical |
| — | Audience and channel for the asset | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), and (c)/(d) flagged not assessed — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a), § 11(1) no. 7 — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- BGH substantiation standard for device efficacy claims — **[verify]**, declined above, not sourced

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**Three things to ask counsel**, since you were already heading toward the case law:

1. What evidentiary standard applies to a quantified efficacy claim for a Class IIa device in German-market advertising, and does it differ from the standard for medicinal products?
2. Does a bare "40% faster" with no stated comparator constitute vergleichende Werbung under UWG § 6(1) in the wound-dressing market, or does it fall to § 5 alone?
3. If the assessed intended purpose does not include accelerated healing, does an acceleration claim require a change to the conformity assessment before it can be advertised?

The case-law answer to (1) is the one you actually asked me for — and the one I'd want sourced rather than recalled.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
Two caveats before the substance: this is general legal information, not legal advice — for a market-facing claim in Germany you want a German `Wettbewerbsrecht`/`Medizinprodukterecht` lawyer to sign off. And I'm working from memory without live access to the case databases here, so treat the paragraph-level wording below as a paraphrase to verify against the published judgment text (I can draft a verification list for your counsel).

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil vom 6.2.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649).

It concerned a medicinal product, but the German courts apply its standard to all `gesundheitsbezogene Werbung`, medical devices included. It is the case that gets cited in essentially every medical device efficacy-claim dispute.

## The standard it set

1. **Heightened scrutiny.** Because health is a high-ranking legal interest and misleading claims can cause real harm, health-related advertising faces "besonders strenge Anforderungen an die Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit" of the statement.

2. **The substantive test: `gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis`.** A health-related efficacy claim is misleading (§ 3 HWG, § 5 UWG) unless it is covered by *secured* scientific knowledge **at the time the advertising is published**. Plausibility, mechanism-of-action reasoning, or "the best evidence we currently have" does not meet it.

3. **Reversed burden of proof — this is the part that decides cases.** The claimant (competitor or `Wettbewerbszentrale`) need only show that the claim is scientifically *unproven or disputed*. The advertiser then bears the full `Darlegungs- und Beweislast` that the claim is scientifically secured. This is a deliberate departure from the normal UWG allocation, and it means you lose by default if your evidence is thin.

4. **What the underlying study must look like.** Where the advertiser relies on (or the ad implies) study evidence, the study must satisfy the principles of evidence-based medicine: in principle a **randomised, placebo-/comparator-controlled, double-blind trial with an adequate number of subjects and adequate statistical analysis, published so that it has entered the professional discourse** (`in den Diskussionsprozess der Fachwelt einbezogen`). A methodologically weak study cannot support a strong claim.

5. **No overstating the study.** The claim may not go beyond what the study actually establishes — and the advertiser may not conceal the study's own limitations (open-label design, secondary or post-hoc endpoint, the authors' own caveats). Selectively quoting a favourable number from a study whose authors qualified it is itself misleading.

6. **Continuing obligation.** The advertiser carries the risk if the scientific basis is later undermined; the claim must be withdrawn when the substantiation falls away.

Supporting older authority for the burden shift: **BGH, GRUR 1991, 848 – "Rheumalind II"**.

## Applied to "Heilt Wunden 40 % schneller" with n=12, unpublished

This claim fails on every limb, and not marginally:

| Requirement | Your evidence |
|---|---|
| Randomised, controlled, blinded | unlikely in an in-house study — needs checking |
| Adequate n / statistical power | n=12 cannot support a 40 % quantified effect |
| Published, peer-discussed | no — fails element 4 outright |
| Claim ≤ study finding | a precise "40 %" from n=12 is overstatement per se |

Two additional independent problems:

- **Comparative claim.** "40 % faster" *than what* — standard of care? a named competitor? no dressing? An undefined baseline triggers § 5a UWG, and if it's a comparison with an identifiable competitor, § 6 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 UWG requires objectively verifiable comparison of relevant features.
- **MDR Art. 7.** Since 2021 this is the primary prohibition on misleading medical device claims — ascribing performance the device doesn't have, or misleading as to clinical benefit. A breach also feeds § 3a UWG as a `Marktverhaltensregel`. Separately, check the claim stays inside the **CE-certified intended purpose** and is supported by your clinical evaluation under Annex XIV; a claim beyond the intended purpose is a regulatory problem on top of the advertising one.

Realistic exposure: `Abmahnung` from a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale, demand for a `Unterlassungserklärung` with contractual penalty, costs — and the reversed burden means the n=12 study is what you'd have to defend in court.

## What I'd do instead

Drop the quantified comparative claim. Viable directions, roughly in order of safety:

1. Claims confined to the CE-certified intended purpose and the device's documented mode of action (moisture management, exudate handling, barrier function) — no comparative speed claim.
2. If you want to use the study at all, restrict it to `Fachkreise` communication, fully disclosed as an exploratory in-house observation with n=12, framed as a hypothesis, no percentage headline. Note § 11 HWG constrains what study references you can put in lay-facing advertising.
3. If "faster healing" is commercially essential, treat it as an evidence project: a properly powered, controlled, published RCT against a defined comparator. That's the only route to a defensible quantified claim under this standard.

Want me to draft a set of compliant German claim variants at each of those three levels, plus the verification checklist (exact BGH wording, MDR Art. 7 text, § 11 HWG scope for medical devices) for your counsel to confirm?

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
I can't run a legal database search from here, so the citations below are from memory. Treat the case numbers as leads to pull from juris/beck-online before anything goes in a file — I've flagged my confidence on each.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urt. v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649). *High confidence on existence and holding; verify the exact date.*

This is the reference decision for substantiation of health-related efficacy claims. The standard it set, in the terms the court used:

1. **Gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis.** A health-related efficacy claim is misleading (§ 5 UWG, § 3 HWG) if it does not correspond to secured scientific knowledge *at the time the advertising is published*. Acquiring the evidence later does not cure it.

2. **The gold-standard formula.** Where the advertiser claims scientific proof, the proof must in principle come from a *"randomisierte, placebokontrollierte Doppelblindstudie mit einer adäquaten statistischen Auswertung, die durch die Veröffentlichung in den Diskussionsprozess der Fachwelt einbezogen worden ist."* Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, adequately powered and statistically analysed, **and published** so the scientific community has had the chance to engage with it.

3. **Reversal of the burden.** Normally the plaintiff proves the misleading character. In health advertising the BGH reverses it: once the plaintiff asserts the claim lacks scientific support, **the advertiser bears the full Darlegungs- und Beweislast** that the statement is scientifically secured. (Line runs back through *Vorbeugen mit Coffein!*, BGH GRUR 2010, 359 — *medium confidence on that citation*.)

4. **Umstrittene Meinung.** Advertising with a scientifically contested proposition is unlawful unless the opposing view is disclosed. Refined in **BGH, Urt. v. 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"** (*medium-high confidence*), which also confirms that a non-RCT design can suffice only exceptionally, where an RCT is not feasible and the deviation is justified.

5. **Strengeprinzip.** Standing case law: health advertising is subject to particularly strict requirements as to accuracy, clarity and unambiguousness, because the protected interest is health.

**Medical-device-specific:** **BGH, Urt. v. 28.01.2016 – I ZR 36/14 – "Feuchtigkeitsspendendes Gel-Reservoir"** (*medium confidence on the details*) is the one to pull — it applies the same strict regime to medical devices and addresses the argument that CE conformity assessment substantiates the claim. It does not. The certificate has no Tatbestandswirkung for the civil court assessing misleading advertising.

## Applied to your facts

Your claim fails this standard, and not marginally.

- **n=12, unpublished, in-house** meets none of the four gold-standard elements. Unpublished alone is dispositive under the *Basisinsulin* formula — it has never entered the "Diskussionsprozess der Fachwelt."
- **"40% faster" is a quantified claim**, which raises the bar rather than lowering it. A precise figure represents to the reader that a precise measurement exists.
- **Faster than what?** No comparator is stated. That is independently attackable either as an unclear Spitzenstellungsbehauptung or, if a comparator is implied, as vergleichende Werbung under § 6 UWG requiring an objective, verifiable, representative comparison.
- **Regulatory layer on top of UWG:** Art. 7 MDR prohibits misleading claims and is a Marktverhaltensregelung within § 3a UWG. Separately, the claim must be covered by your clinical evaluation (Art. 61, Annex XIV) and must not exceed the intended purpose in your technical documentation and IFU. A healing-rate superiority claim that isn't in your intended purpose is a notified-body problem as well as an advertising problem — potentially a change requiring re-assessment for a Class IIa device.
- **HWG** applies to medical devices via § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a; § 3 S. 2 Nr. 1 covers attributing efficacy the product does not have.

Enforcement in Germany is cheap and fast for the other side: competitors and Wettbewerbszentrale/Verbände under § 8 Abs. 3 UWG, Abmahnung plus strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung, then Ordnungsgeld on repetition. This is the kind of copy that draws one.

## Realistic options

**Drop the number.** Qualitative claims tied to the mechanism actually documented in your technical file ("supports moist wound healing") sit far safer, provided they match the intended purpose.

**Keep the study, change the audience and the framing.** Fachkreise communication of your own data, presented transparently as a single-arm in-house pilot with n=12 and no comparator, is a different act from consumer advertising with a bare "40%." Still not risk-free, and it cannot be laundered back into the pack copy.

**Run the study that supports the claim.** If "40% faster" is commercially important, an RCT against the relevant standard-of-care comparator, published, is the only route to a defensible version of that sentence.

I'd take option one for launch and start scoping option three in parallel. Get a German Wettbewerbsrecht/Medizinprodukterecht specialist to sign off before print — I'm giving you the doctrinal shape, not legal advice, and the case citations need verification.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
Short answer: there is no device-specific BGH landmark. The controlling standard comes from the BGH's health-advertising line, and it applies to Medizinprodukte because § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG brings medical devices inside the HWG's scope.

**Note on verification:** I have no web access in this session, so the citations below are from memory. Have counsel pull the originals before you rely on them in a risk memo.

## Leading case

**BGH, Urt. v. 6.2.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649)

This is the case German practitioners cite for the substantiation standard. The follow-on **BGH, Urt. v. 7.5.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"** confirms and sharpens it.

## The standard it set

Four elements:

**1. Strengeprinzip.** Health-related advertising is subject to "besonders strenge Anforderungen an die Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit" of the claim, because errors here damage health, not just wallets.

**2. Gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis.** A claim is misleading under § 3 HWG / § 5 UWG if it does not correspond to secured scientific knowledge **at the time the advertisement runs**. Generating the evidence later does not cure it.

**3. Study-quality (the "gold standard").** Where the advertiser relies on a study, the study must meet the recognised rules of scientific research. That means, as a rule: randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, adequately powered, evaluated **against the pre-specified protocol and primary endpoint**, and published so that it has entered the scientific discourse. The specific holding in *Basisinsulin* was that a result taken from a **secondary endpoint / post-hoc analysis** not pre-specified in the protocol cannot carry the claim.

**4. The advertising must not exceed what the study actually shows.** If you cite a study, the claim must stay strictly within its demonstrated result — no extrapolation, no rounding up, no generalising beyond the studied population and indication.

**Burden of proof.** This is the part that usually decides the case. Normally the plaintiff proves the claim is misleading. In health advertising, once the advertiser presents a scientifically contested proposition as settled, **the burden flips to the advertiser** to prove scientific backing. In practice, in an einstweilige Verfügung, you are the one who has to produce the evidence on short notice.

## Applied to your facts

"Heals wounds 40% faster" backed by n=12, in-house, unpublished, fails on essentially every element:

- **n=12** will not be treated as adequately powered for a quantified 40% effect. Effect-size precision at that n is very poor.
- **Unpublished** means it has not entered the scientific discussion and cannot be scrutinised — under this line of case law that alone largely disqualifies it as proof of *gesicherte* Erkenntnis.
- **In-house** goes to independence; not automatically fatal, but it removes any benefit of the doubt.
- **"40%" is a quantified claim**, which raises rather than lowers the bar. The BGH requires the number to be precisely what the study established.
- **Faster than what?** The comparator is missing. An unanchored comparative is independently misleading under § 5 UWG, and if a competitor is identifiable, § 6 UWG comparative-advertising rules bite too.

**Second, separate exposure:** Art. 7 MDR prohibits claims that mislead as to performance, and the claim must be covered by your clinical evaluation (Art. 61, Annex XIV) and stay within the CE-certified intended purpose. A 40% healing-rate claim not in your clinical evaluation is a regulatory problem with your notified body / BfArM, independent of the competition-law risk.

**Who comes after you:** in Germany, realistically a competitor, the Wettbewerbszentrale, or the Verband Sozialer Wettbewerb via § 8 Abs. 3 Nr. 2 UWG — Abmahnung plus strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung, often followed by an einstweilige Verfügung within weeks. VSW is very active on wound-care claims specifically.

## What would actually be defensible

Either invest in an adequately powered, randomised, controlled, published study with faster healing as the **pre-specified primary endpoint** and a named comparator — or drop the efficacy claim and market on mechanism/properties that your technical documentation already supports (moisture management, exudate handling, atraumatic removal, wear time), phrased as device characteristics rather than a quantified clinical outcome.

I'd treat the current copy as not shippable in Germany as written. Have German regulatory/competition counsel sign off before launch.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy, continuous ECG patch

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Continuous ECG patch, Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does not apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 optional reword, 2 to verify, 1 OK.

**No breaches identified** against the provisions this review verifies. The copy tracks the intended purpose closely, states the supervision condition, and — importantly — puts no performance figures on the page. Both open items are questions for the technical file, not defects in the drafting.

**Ready to publish:** see the gate at the end.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A wear-duration spec is not an intended-purpose extension — the assessed purpose says "continuous" without a stated ceiling, so 14 days neither contradicts it nor suggests a use outside it. "Up to" is properly hedged.
**Evidence needed:** The validated maximum wear duration from the technical documentation (adhesive/skin-contact biocompatibility over that period, battery, signal quality at the tail end). Confirm 14 days is the *validated* figure, not the theoretical battery life.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*wesentliche Merkmale*, *Zwecktauglichkeit*) `[verified]`, **if** the validated wear duration is shorter than 14 days, or if 14 days is achievable only under conditions the copy doesn't state.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is asserted, so there's nothing to be misled by on the face of the copy. For a Fachkreise audience this is the conservative form — better than a bare "98% sensitivity" with no population or comparator.
**Evidence needed:** That the data pack actually exists and is fulfilled on request; that it describes the study population, reference standard and arrhythmia types; and that it relates to the **current** CE-certified device and algorithm version, not a predecessor.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1, limb "*Ergebnisse oder wesentliche Bestandteile von Tests*" `[verified]`, **if** the pack that goes out is cherry-picked — e.g. AF-only figures presented as covering "cardiac arrhythmias" generally, or figures without the essential study conditions.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Reproduces the assessed intended purpose almost verbatim, including the supervision condition. Nothing here ascribes a function beyond it.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK — with one optional tightening

**Optional reword (limb (d) hygiene):** The assessed purpose is limited to **adults**; the copy is silent on population. Silence is not a suggestion of paediatric use, so I don't read this as an Art. 7(d) breach. But a cardiology trade-press readership includes paediatric cardiologists, the restriction is part of the assessed purpose, and restoring it costs two words.

**Paste-ready revision (English, as supplied):**

> "Continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults for up to 14 days. For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."

Two changes: "in adults" restored, and "continuous" restored from the assessed purpose. If this runs in German, the German wording is the version that must be reviewed — a translation can drift on exactly these words, and I've only seen the English.

## Open question I can't close from what I have

**MDR Art. 7(c)** — failing to inform of a likely risk — is an omission test, and I won't infer a risk from the device category to manufacture a finding. The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking the IFU for anything in the skin-contact/wear-duration area, and for any stated limitation on what single-lead recording can resolve.

Two things reduce the exposure as drafted: the copy states the supervision condition, which conveys that output requires clinical interpretation; and trade-press copy isn't expected to carry patient-facing safety text. If the IFU does record a likely risk, an IFU pointer in the asset is usually the proportionate fix at this length.

## Not engaged

- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** (guaranteed success): nothing promises a certain outcome. "For the detection of" is a purpose statement, not a guarantee. `[verified]`
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b)** (no harmful effects): no side-effect reassurance in the copy. `[verified]`
- **HWG § 11**: audience is Fachkreise, so § 11 does not apply. For what it's worth, the copy carries no no. 7 health-improvement framing either, so repurposing it to an ungated public page wouldn't trip that item on its current wording — but that would be a fresh review, not an inherited clearance. `[verified]`
- **UWG § 6**: no comparison, express or implied. `[verified]`
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4**: the copy makes no class, notified-body or certification claim. If the finished asset carries a CE mark, NB number or certification badge, send me the artwork — those graphics are in scope and this text extract doesn't show them.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear duration; conditions it assumes | RA/QA — technical documentation |
| "data available on request" | The fulfilment pack: population, reference standard, arrhythmia types covered, device/algorithm version | Clinical affairs |
| (c) open question | IFU check for any likely risk or stated limitation | RA/QA — current IFU |

## Provisions cited

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy, continuous ECG patch

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Continuous single-lead ECG patch, **Class IIa** (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias"
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 0 substantiate, 2 OK subject to verification.

This is close to clean. The copy tracks the assessed intended purpose, carries the supervision condition rather than dropping it, and makes no bare performance assertion. One element of the intended purpose has gone missing, and two items rest on material I haven't seen.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** The copy as a whole — "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** The assessed intended purpose is limited to **adults**. The copy states the indication and the supervision condition but carries no population limit, so on its face it suggests use in a population the conformity assessment did not cover. Art. 7(d) prohibits "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out" — and paediatric use of an arrhythmia-detection patch is a use a cardiology readership could plausibly read in.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. This is the limb (d) cure path: narrow the claim, or extend the conformity assessment.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") — the UWG mirror of the same defect, relevant because that is the route an Abmahnung would take.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** insert "in adults" — see paste-ready copy below.

I'd flag the strength of this one honestly: it is an omission rather than an affirmative statement of paediatric use, and it is the weaker shape of a (d) finding. I'm raising it because the fix costs two words and the exposure it removes is the expensive kind.

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Wear duration is a performance characteristic, not part of the intended-purpose wording, so its absence from the intended purpose is not itself a defect. Nothing in the claim conflicts with the assessed purpose — "continuous ... recording" is consistent with a stated maximum wear time.
**Evidence needed:** the validated maximum wear duration from the technical documentation — adhesive wear time, battery life, and signal-quality data out to 14 days, whichever is the binding constraint. "Up to" does not rescue a figure the file does not support.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("wesentliche Merkmale", "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse"), **if** 14 days exceeds the validated wear duration or is achievable only under conditions the copy does not state.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** It states that data exists and is obtainable; it asserts no figure and no threshold. On the material supplied there is nothing misleading in it, and offering the data rather than cherry-picking a number is the safer construction.
**Evidence needed:** confirm (i) the data exists in a form that can actually be released on request, and (ii) what it is derived from. Clinical performance in the claimed indication is what a cardiology readership will assume; bench testing or performance against an annotated database is a materially different thing.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**"), **if** what gets sent on request is bench or database performance that the copy leaves the reader to read as clinical, or if the request route is not honoured in practice.
**Call:** Verify

---

### Limb (c): open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation. I'm not raising a (c) finding, because I haven't seen the IFU and I won't infer a likely risk from the device category — every benefit-framed ad omits some inferable risk, and a finding built that way can't be falsified. Two things make the position defensible as it stands: the copy retains "under healthcare professional supervision", which does surface that clinical involvement is required, and trade-press copy isn't expected to carry patient-facing safety text.

Worth checking against the IFU: if it records a likely risk or a material limitation of single-lead recording for this indication, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix at this length.

### Not engaged

- **HWG § 3** `[verified]` — no guarantee of success (no. 2(a)), no no-harmful-effects claim (no. 2(b)), no claims about the manufacturer's credentials (no. 3(b)).
- **HWG § 11** `[verified]` — Fachkreise. Trade press falls squarely inside. **Conditional:** if this copy is reused on an ungated web page, § 11 nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 come into scope. As written it would likely survive no. 7 anyway — there's no health-improvement or fear-of-not-using framing — but the audience determination should be re-made per placement, not inherited.
- **UWG § 6** `[verified]` — no comparison, express or implied.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** `[verified]` — the copy makes no class, CE, or notified-body claim. If a "Class IIa" or CE badge accompanies the text in the final layout, send me the layout; badges are in scope for Art. 7 and § 5(2) no. 4.

## Paste-ready revised copy

> Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For use **in adults**, under healthcare professional supervision, in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data available on request.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Validated maximum wear duration — adhesive, battery, signal quality | RA / technical documentation owner |
| "sensitivity and specificity data" | The dataset itself; whether clinical or bench/database; a working request route | Clinical affairs |
| Limb (c) | Whether the IFU records a likely risk or material limitation that belongs in a trade-press asset | RA / IFU owner |
| Placement | Confirm every placement is Fachkreise-gated, not an open web page | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3, § 11(1) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4; § 6 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## On clearing this for publication

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify, once "in adults" is restored and the two verification items come back clean. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis.

**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

**Breach:** none
