# Device Claims Review: headline + subline

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-17
**Device:** Class I reusable surgical retractor (Class I, self-certified — no notified body involved)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU rules apply throughout)

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword outright, 1 substantiate, 1 verify against page context.

**Ready to publish: With changes below.**

No MDR Art. 7 limb is breached on the material supplied — the copy ascribes no function, property, or clinical benefit to the device, and suggests no use outside the assessed intended purpose. The exposure here is German unfair-competition exposure on an unsupported popularity claim, not Art. 7.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** It ascribes no function or property to the device (so not Art. 7(a)), and creates no impression about treatment or diagnosis (not (b)). It is an assertion about user acceptance, not about performance.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 sentence 1 ("Unzulässig ist eine irreführende Werbung") and UWG § 5(1) with § 5(2) no. 1 ("wesentlichen Merkmale … Vorteile") — **if** there is no basis at all for the claim, or if the basis is something narrower than "surgeons" generally (e.g. three users at one pilot site). Directed at procurement, an acceptance claim is capable of moving a purchasing decision, which is the § 5(1) materiality hook.
**Evidence needed:** The actual basis — user-preference survey, evaluation-site feedback, n, respondent group, date. If no such basis exists, the claim cannot be cured by evidence and should be narrowed to what you do hold.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

> Note on the puffery question: whether a German reader takes "Surgeons love it" as a factual claim about user acceptance or as non-actionable advertising exaggeration is exactly the line drawn by case law, which this review does not assess. I am not going to tell you which side it lands on. The cheap route is to make the statement either verifiably sourced or obviously non-factual, so the question never has to be answered.

---

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Subjective preference with no clinical or performance content. No Art. 7 limb reaches it, and HWG § 3 nos. 1, 2(a), 2(b) and 3(b) are all unengaged — there is no efficacy claim, no promise of certain success, no no-side-effects reassurance, and no claim about the maker.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6. The word "actually" sets the product against unnamed existing retractors. On these two sentences alone no Mitbewerber is *erkennbar* under § 6(1), so § 6 does not bite. But if the published asset puts this line next to a named competitor, a competitor's image, or a "unlike the legacy…" framing, § 6(1) is satisfied and the comparison then has to clear § 6(2) no. 2 — "objektiv … wesentliche, relevante, **nachprüfbare** und typische Eigenschaften". Enjoyment is not a verifiable characteristic, so a comparison built on it would fail no. 2 on the face of the copy, and no amount of internal data fixes that.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — this one is about page context, not data.
**Call:** Verify (send me the full page/panel this sits on)

---

**Limb (c) — open question, not a finding.** The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in the asset — a reusable device typically has reprocessing conditions in its IFU, but I am not going to infer one and flag you for omitting it. Worth checking the IFU; if there is such a condition, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix for a two-line headline, not safety text.

**Drafting note (not a breach).** For a procurement audience, this copy says nothing about the device. It carries no reference to retraction, exposure, open procedures, reprocessing, or instrument set compatibility. That is a sales problem rather than a legal one, but it is the reason the only legally interesting words in it are the risky ones.

## Paste-ready revision

If you hold real evaluation feedback, name it:

> **Preferred by 18 of 20 surgeons in clinical evaluation at [site], [month/year].**
> Manual tissue retraction for open procedures — balanced grip, full reprocessing cycle validated.

If you do not hold it, drop the acceptance claim and sell the attribute:

> **Built for the hand that holds it.**
> Manual tissue retraction to maintain surgical site exposure in open procedures. Reusable, fully reprocessable.

German, same two options:

> **Von 18 von 20 Chirurgen in der klinischen Bewertung an [Klinik], [Monat/Jahr] bevorzugt.**
> Manuelle Gewebe-Retraktion für offene Eingriffe — ausbalancierter Griff, validierte Aufbereitung.

> **Für die Hand gemacht, die ihn führt.**
> Manuelle Retraktion von Gewebe zur Aufrechterhaltung der Sicht auf das Operationsfeld bei offenen Eingriffen. Wiederverwendbar, vollständig aufbereitbar.

Both versions track the assessed intended purpose verbatim, which keeps limb (d) clean.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it." | Survey/evaluation basis: n, respondent group, site, date, question asked | Clinical affairs / sales ops |
| "…you'll actually enjoy using." | Full asset context — is any competitor identifiable on the same page? | Marketing |
| (c) omission check | Does the IFU record a likely risk or reprocessing limitation? | RA / technical documentation owner |

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 sentence 1, § 3 nos. 1, 2(a), 2(b), 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) — noted as inapplicable (Fachkreise) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 — not engaged; the copy makes no certification, class, or notified-body claim `[verified]`

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. **Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none

Whether a sentence like this reads as a checkable factual claim or as permissible advertising exaggeration turns on case law, which this review does not assess — so I can't call that for you.
**Evidence needed:** A user survey, OP-team evaluation, or reference-customer data with n, sites, and date — or drop the aggregate framing.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."

- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (third-party statements):** § 11 applies only *außerhalb der Fachkreise*. The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs here — for a reusable instrument, reprocessing and reuse-cycle limits are the obvious place to look, but I'd be inferring that from the device category rather than reading it in your documentation, and that's not a basis for a finding. Worth checking against the IFU.

Proportionality note: a two-line trade headline is not expected to carry safety text. If (c) does bite, the proportionate fix is an IFU pointer, not a risk paragraph.

**Option A — keep it light, remove the substantiation burden entirely** (nothing to prove, nothing to verify):

## Verdict

Not usable as written. Two short sentences, and both are claims that German advertising law will treat as requiring proof — while neither says anything about what the device does.

## Issues

| # | Copy element | Problem | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Surgeons love it." | Unsubstantiated general-consensus/testimonial claim. Implies broad professional endorsement without naming a source, sample, or method. Health-sector advertising carries a heightened substantiation burden in German case law, and the burden sits with the advertiser. | § 3 HWG (Irreführung), § 5 UWG, MPDG § 14, MDR Art. 7 |
| 2 | "Surgeons love it." | If this copy ever appears anywhere publicly accessible (website, trade-fair banner, downloadable brochure without gating), it stops being Fachkreiswerbung and becomes Publikumswerbung — where advertising with professional recommendation / third-party statements is restricted. Procurement brochures leak into open channels routinely. | § 11 Abs. 1 HWG (esp. Nr. 2, Nr. 11), § 2 HWG |
| 3 | "you'll actually enjoy using" | "Actually" implies competing retractors are unpleasant to use — blanket disparagement of the product category. No competitor is identified, so § 6 UWG probably doesn't bite, but pauschale Herabsetzung remains exposed. | § 4 Nr. 1 UWG |
| 4 | Both sentences | Zero connection to the declared intended purpose. Nothing about retraction, exposure, stability, or open procedures. MDR Art. 7 requires claims not to mislead as to intended purpose, safety, or performance; an ad built purely on affect, with no performance substance, is weak on its own terms and unsupported by technical documentation. | MDR Art. 7(a)–(d) |
| 5 | Both sentences | Any usability/satisfaction claim must trace to a record — usability engineering file (IEC 62366-1), clinical evaluation (MDR Annex XIV), or a documented user survey. If no such record exists, the claim cannot be made at all, in any wording. | MDR Annex II/XIV |
| 6 | Register | Consumer-brand tone aimed at hospital procurement. Procurement decides on material, reprocessing validation, cycle life, instrument-tray compatibility, UDI/GTIN, price. "Enjoy" is not a line item in a Vergabeunterlage. | Commercial, not legal |
| 7 | Language | English copy into the German market. Permissible for Fachkreise, but if the device is presented as CE-marked in the same material, note that a reusable surgical instrument is Class Ir — the notified body number must accompany the CE mark, and reprocessing validation is NB-assessed. Worth checking the asset isn't showing a bare CE mark. | MDR Art. 52(7)(a), Annex VIII Rule 6 |

## Rewrite

**If you have survey data** (this is the version I'd ship):

> **Stabile Exposition, verlässlicher Zugang.**
> Wundspreizer zur manuellen Geweberetraktion bei offenen Eingriffen.
> In einer Anwenderbefragung an [n] Kliniken bewerteten [x] % der befragten Chirurginnen und Chirurgen die Handhabung als „gut" oder „sehr gut" ([Erhebungszeitraum], Methodik auf Anfrage).

Name the sample, the period, and offer the method. That converts issue 1 from a liability into a differentiator, and it survives a channel change to Publikumswerbung far better than "Surgeons love it."

**If you have no survey data**, drop the satisfaction angle entirely and sell the verifiable attributes:

> **Griffgeometrie für lange Eingriffe. Validierte Aufbereitung.**
> Wundspreizer zur manuellen Geweberetraktion bei offenen Eingriffen. [Material/Legierung], Aufbereitung validiert nach DIN EN ISO 17664, [Anzahl] validierte Aufbereitungszyklen, kompatibel mit [Siebsystem].

## Two things to confirm before this goes out

1. **Does the survey/usability record exist?** Everything in option 1 depends on it. If the "surgeons love it" line came from sales anecdote rather than a documented source, option 2 is your only path.
2. **Where will this asset live?** Gated Fachkreise portal vs. open website changes which HWG provisions apply. Assume open unless access control is actually enforced.

Note: this is a compliance review of the copy, not legal advice — have your RA/legal function sign off on the final wording.

Don't run it as written. There's no MDR Article 7 problem in the classic sense — the copy makes no clinical, safety, or performance claim, so it doesn't stray outside the intended purpose or ascribe functions the device lacks. The problems are elsewhere: one unsubstantiated factual claim, one implied superiority claim, and a channel risk that could turn the first line into a per-se HWG violation.

## Finding 1 — "Surgeons love it" is a verifiable factual claim

This reads as an assertion about user opinion, not as obvious puffery. German courts treat that as objectively checkable, and in health-related advertising the burden of substantiation sits with the advertiser at a high standard (the *Strengeprinzip* line of BGH case law). Unsubstantiated, it's exposed under UWG §5 and HWG §3.

Two further wrinkles:

- **If you do have survey data**, HWG §6 requires the citation to be traceable — author, date, exact wording, and it must be current and representative. "Surgeons love it" summarizing an n=12 advisory board won't survive the generalization.
- **If any of these surgeons are compensated** (KOLs, advisory board, consultancy), you need commercial-intent disclosure under UWG §5a Abs. 4, plus whatever transfer-of-value obligations apply.

## Finding 2 — "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using" implies superiority

"The retractor" (definite article) plus "actually" carries a comparison: other retractors are not enjoyable to use. That's an implicit *Alleinstellungsbehauptung* against unnamed competitors, which pulls in UWG §6 (comparative advertising) and edges toward §4 Nr. 1 (*Herabsetzung*). Implied comparison is still comparison — you don't get a pass for leaving the competitor unnamed.

"Enjoy using" on its own is closer to permissible puffery, but the construction around it is what creates the claim.

## Finding 3 — the Fachkreise gate is load-bearing

Your §11 HWG exposure depends entirely on the audience staying professional. §11 Abs. 1 restricts advertising directed at the general public, including advertising with professional recommendations (Nr. 2) and with third-party testimonials or references to them (Nr. 11). "Surgeons love it" sits squarely in that territory.

So: in a gated procurement portal or a tender document, §11 doesn't apply. On an ungated product webpage, in trade press, or on LinkedIn, it plausibly does — and then the line is problematic regardless of how good your survey data is. Confirm the channel before this goes anywhere. (Scope of individual §11 subsections for devices rather than medicinal products is not uniformly settled; treat this as a reason to gate, not a reason to gamble.)

## Localization

Don't translate this literally. "Den Sie wirklich gerne benutzen" lands badly in German B2B medtech register — it reads as trivializing a surgical instrument to a procurement committee. Also: if you go with "Chirurgen," use "Operateurinnen und Operateure" or "Anwenderinnen und Anwender," which is now standard in German clinical B2B copy.

## Rewrites

**Option A — substantiate and keep the social proof:**
> "In einer Anwenderbefragung an [X] Kliniken (n=[X], [Monat/Jahr]) bewerteten [X] % der Operateure Handhabung und Griffergonomie mit 'gut' oder 'sehr gut'."

Cite the study inline or by footnote. Only viable if the survey is real, current, and reasonably representative — and only in a gated channel.

**Option B — drop the emotive frame, speak to procurement:**
> "Ergonomischer Griff für ermüdungsfreies Halten bei langen Eingriffen. Validierte Aufbereitung nach [ISO 17664], [X] Aufbereitungszyklen."

This is the stronger option. A procurement committee is buying reprocessing validation, cycle life, tray compatibility, and total cost of ownership. Neither of your current sentences gives them a single decision input.

**Safe-harbour version of your existing line**, if you want to keep the tone:
> "Entwickelt mit Operateuren. Für ermüdungsfreies Halten."

"Entwickelt mit" is a process statement about your own development — defensible with design-history documentation, and it makes no claim about what surgeons feel.

## Before publishing

Keep a claims substantiation file alongside the technical documentation: for each claim, the evidence, its date, and the reviewer who signed off. Worth doing because enforcement in Germany is mostly private — a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale sends an *Abmahnung* with a *strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung*, and the cost and disruption arrive long before any authority does.

Have the final German wording reviewed by counsel; I've flagged the exposure, but the §11 device-scope question and the sufficiency of your specific survey data are judgment calls that want a lawyer's name on them.

## Verdict

Not usable as written. Two short sentences carry three distinct problems: an unsubstantiated collective endorsement, an implicit disparaging comparison, and zero content for the actual buyer. None of it is fatal — it's fixable — but it needs a rewrite rather than a tweak.

(Regulatory read, not legal advice — have your RA/legal sign off before release.)

## Findings

**1. "Surgeons love it" — unsubstantiated endorsement claim**

The good news: because the audience is Fachkreise, **§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 11 HWG** (ban on third-party testimonials, recommendations, letters of appreciation) does not bite — that provision applies only to advertising *außerhalb der Fachkreise*. Hospital procurement qualifies as Fachkreise under **§ 2 HWG** ("Einrichtungen, die der Gesundheit von Menschen dienen").

The bad news: **§ 3 HWG** (irreführende Werbung), **§ 5 UWG**, and **Art. 7 MDR** apply regardless of audience. A blanket "surgeons love it" is a factual assertion about user acceptance. Without data behind it, it's misleading and attackable — typically by a competitor via Abmahnung, which is the realistic enforcement route here, not an authority.

Two caveats on the Fachkreise exemption:
- It only holds if the channel is **genuinely gated**. An open website with the copy publicly crawlable is Publikumswerbung in practice, and then Nr. 11 does apply. Put it behind a Fachkreis gate (login/DocCheck) or at minimum a prominent, unavoidable "Nur für Fachkreise" interstitial.
- If you substantiate the claim by pointing to a survey or study, **§ 6 HWG** kicks in: you must name the author, the date of publication, and quote the wording accurately.

**2. "actually" — implicit comparative disparagement**

This is the sharpest exposure and the easiest to miss. "The retractor you'll **actually** enjoy using" only works rhetorically by asserting that other retractors are unpleasant to use. That is implied comparative advertising against the entire market, measured on a criterion that isn't objectively verifiable.

Engages **§ 6 Abs. 2 Nr. 2 UWG** (comparisons must relate to objectively verifiable, relevant characteristics) and **Nr. 5** (no Herabsetzung of competitors). Delete the word; the sentence loses nothing you can defend anyway.

**3. "enjoy using" — low regulatory risk, high commercial waste**

As a purely subjective preference statement it ascribes no medical function, so **Art. 7(b) MDR** is not really in play. But it's the wrong currency for this audience. Procurement doesn't buy enjoyment — it evaluates cost per use, service life, reprocessing validation, tender criteria (VgV/GWB for public hospitals), and availability. You've spent the whole headline on the one stakeholder who doesn't sign the order.

**4. Nothing anchors the claim to the intended purpose**

Under **Art. 7 MDR** claims must stay inside the declared intended purpose. Your copy says nothing at all, so it doesn't *breach* this — but it also gives a reviewer nothing to check against the technical documentation. Intended-purpose language ("manuelle Retraktion von Gewebe zur Offenhaltung des OP-Feldes bei offenen Eingriffen") should appear verbatim and consistently across collateral, IFU, and declaration of conformity.

**5. Classification point worth checking before any CE artwork ships**

A reusable surgical retractor is almost certainly a **reusable surgical instrument → Class Ir**, not plain Class I. Under Art. 52(7)(a) MDR that requires notified body involvement limited to reprocessing, and the **CE mark must be accompanied by the NB identification number**. If your collateral shows a bare CE logo, or your file is self-certified as plain Class I, that's a bigger problem than the copy. Worth confirming with RA.

**6. Language**

IFU and labelling must be German for the German market (MDR Annex I 23.1(f) + MPDG). Marketing copy isn't strictly mandated, but English headlines for German hospital procurement are a conversion problem regardless.

## What's missing that this audience actually wants

Reprocessing validation per **ISO 17664** and the number of validated cycles; material spec (e.g. stainless steel per **ISO 7153-1**); autoclave parameters and compatibility with existing tray/container systems; sizes and blade geometries; delivery state (non-sterile, sterilize before first use); article numbers, Basic UDI-DI/UDI-DI; expected service life and cost per use; availability and lead times.

## Rewrite

**Option A — claim-free, tender-ready (recommended):**

> **Retraktion, die im Sieb bleibt.**
> Wundhaltehaken zur manuellen Retraktion von Gewebe und Offenhaltung des Operationsfeldes bei offenen Eingriffen. Wiederverwendbar, validiert aufbereitbar nach ISO 17664 — ausgelegt für [X] Aufbereitungszyklen. [Material] nach ISO 7153-1, kompatibel mit Standard-Siebkörben.

**Option B — keeps the ergonomics angle, substantiated:**

> **Ergonomisch halten. Wirtschaftlich aufbereiten.**
> Griffgeometrie für ermüdungsarmes Halten über lange Eingriffe. In einer Anwenderbefragung unter [n] Chirurg:innen ([Monat/Jahr], [Methode]) bewerteten [x] % den Haltekomfort mit "gut" oder "sehr gut".

Note that "ermüdungsarm" is itself a performance claim and needs evidence in the technical documentation — don't treat it as free copy.

## If you keep any user-acceptance claim

You need, in the file and retrievable: survey population and n, date, method and question wording, and the actual result. Cite author/date/wording in the ad per § 6 HWG. Route the underlying feedback into your **PMCF** plan so the marketing claim and the post-market data tell the same story — a mismatch between the two is exactly what an auditor pulls on.
